Madam Speaker, I am rising pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present yet another batch of petitions from Victoria against the goods and services tax.
We have already had thousands of signatures on petitions urging the rejection of this tax, and here are some more. The tide has not yet ceased. The people of Victoria, in overwhelming numbers, are asking the government to back off this unfair tax and to reform the tax system in a much fairer way than is presently proposed.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition with several hundred names of Canadian war veterans who belong to the Royal Canadian Legion branches in Blind River and Espanola, Ontario. They complain that the government has reduced homekeeping services to veterans and substantially increased the cost of long-term care.
They point out that veterans have already given a great service to the country and call on the House of Commons and Parliament of Canada to reject these budget measures that deprive veterans of proper services and increase their financial hardship.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I rise in the House today to present petitions signed by Canadians who are opposed to the goods and services tax.
These petitions were circulated by residents who ask taxpayers to join them in a demonstration on Parliament Hill at noon on Saturday, May 12, to show that Canadians are opposed to the goods and services tax proposed by the government.
To all those who do not speak French, Madam Speaker-

I would like to extend the same invitation; twelve o'clock, Saturday, Parliament Hill.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour and duty, in accordance with Standing Order 36, to present a petition from residents of Toronto; Ottawa; Woodstock, New Brunswick; Saint John; Willowdale and Scarborough, Ontario; and Burnaby, B.C.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to join with the Assembly of First Nations and the Innu of Labrador to demand that the Canadian government end all NATO-NORAD low-level flight training in Canada and oppose the establishment of NATO operations in Canada, including the proposed tactical fighter and weapons training base at Goose Bay.
They ask that Parliament redirect Canada's NATO and NORAD funding toward enabling Canada's aboriginal peoples to regain control of their lands and livelihood, and promoting sustainable development for all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to table a petition, certified correct as to form and content, from members and friends of Branch 83 of the Royal Canadian Legion in Florence, Nova Scotia.
There are 100 signatures, and in part the petition states that the Government of Canada has introduced changes that will reduce homekeeping services to veterans and substantially increase the cost of long-term care.
Whereas the veterans have already given service to this country and should not be targeted by these measures, the petitioners call upon Parliament to reject those budget measures that deprive veterans of proper services and increase their financial hardship.
May 10, 1990

Madam Speaker,
I have the honour to present a petition bearing 50 signatures. The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to stop wasting our tax dollars and to reject the proposed goods and services tax. I fully support that position.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I, too, have a petition which I wish to present to the House. It is signed by people mainly from the Hull, Vanier, and Ottawa areas.
These people call upon Parliament to stop wasting the tax dollars and to reject the goods and services tax. They also invite people to a rally this Saturday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, following in the footsteps of hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are opposed to the government's goods and services tax, today I wish to present another petition signed by Canadians who strenuously object to this tax and who want to come here next Saturday, May 12, to demonstrate their dissatisfaction with a government that wants to saddle Canadians with a new tax that will be regressive and very costly.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour today to present several petitions on behalf of my constituents showing the wide range of their dissatisfaction with the government.
Perhaps the first one I should present is on behalf of the veterans of Canada who fought for their country. They are objecting to the measures in the last budget that will place additional hardships on them by depriving them of proper services and increasing their financial hardship.

Madam Speaker, I have some other petitions from the farmers of Lambton-Middlesex, from Oil Springs, Petrolia, Both-well, Alvinston, Camlachie and Wyoming, and even some from my colleague's riding of Kent.
Routine Proceedings
The petitioners all object to the very high and injurious interest rates that are being imposed upon Canada and the farmers of Canada. They want the government to reinstate the fuel tax rebate and the interest free provisions of the advance payment for crops, to provide fair and equal market access for Canadian farm commodities, and to introduce agricultural policies that will encourage agricultural development in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I also have some other petitions to present. They are signed by various people from across my great riding. They are calling on the government to re-evaluate and upgrade the VIA Rail service cuts that took place across the country on January 1.

Finally, I have petitions from across the riding as well. The petitioners state that the federal government wants to impose on Canadians a new 7 per cent goods and services tax. They point out that this new tax will apply to books, magazines, newspapers, et cetera.
They point out, quite rightly, that this is the first time this would have been done since Confederation. The petitioners call on the government to exempt Canada's books, magazines and newspapers from the proposed goods and services tax.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I rise in the House today to present petitions signed by Canadians who are opposed to the goods and services tax.
These petitions were circulated by residents who ask taxpayers to join them in a demonstration on Parliament Hill at noon on Saturday, May 12, to show that Canadians object to the goods and services tax proposed by the government.

I have several hundred signatures of people involved in and concerned about the whole area of reading. They have brought to our attention that Canada has seen fit, since Confederation and without hiatus, to apply a zero rate of tax to magazines, books and newspapers which are now proposed to be included in the GST. They feel that the uninhibited dissemination of the printed word is

May 10, 1990
Routine Proceedings
a comer-stone of democracy, culture, and education, and that a literary and productive society will be negatively affected by the GST application.
Therefore, the petitioners have asked the House to reaffirm the historic principles embodied in the tax-free status of the printed word by retaining the zero rate in the GST legislation and regulations.
Last, Madam Speaker, also in the interest of the concern around the GST, and perhaps joining us on Saturday on the Hill in the demonstration, will be people who are involved in occupational therapy, physiotherapy, social services, speech language pathology and audiology outside of public institutions.
They call upon Parliament not to impose the goods and services tax on any health care services, whether delivered in public institutions or in the community.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour and privilege, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present some petitions today. One relates to the goods and services tax.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 AGRICULTURAL ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to ask the Chair to rule favourably on my request for an emergency debate concerning the farm crisis, particularly in my own province of Saskatchewan.
I recognize that several of my colleagues in the last few of days have made the same request of the Chair. They have very eloquently and forcefully put forward the position of the farmers who are faced with decreases in
Routine Proceedings
the initial grain prices. Interest rates have increased and various other costs such as transportation costs have risen. There is a real crisis facing farmers today.
There is a new factor that has occurred in the last 24 hours. The Minister of Agriculture and the Premier of Saskatchewan have met. They reported, smiling, when they left the meeting, how happy they were that they had had successful discussions and so forth. Yet, no announcement is planned to be made.
The farmers in my home district and in the province of Saskatchewan in general need to know right away what the situation will be. They have to make decisions yesterday, today, and tomorrow on what their future will be.
Therefore, I ask the Chair to call upon Parliament to debate this issue, to stop this phoney war between the federal and provincial government, and to act so that my constituents and other farmers in Saskatchewan will be able to make their living and put the seed in the ground this year.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today to discuss business that relates to northern Canada. It is a topic that is very dear to my heart. Not too long ago on a supply day, we on this side of the House debated the regional development programs and the effect the lack of those programs has had on northern Ontario and northern Canada and also the parts of Canada not considered to be in the mainstream of Canadian society.
May 10, 1990

I would like to talk today about the problems created by the government in northern Canada and specifically northern Ontario, which I know the best. As is said in the motion in front of us, there are many issues created by government that have affected northern Canada and northern Ontario.
I do not want to re-read the motion because I think it speaks for itself. It concerns the reduction in unemployment insurance, the cuts to VIA Rail to the mainline that ran through northern Ontario, the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber and the cancellation of the mining depletion allowances which has basically made the flow-through share mechanism useless. Finally, and possibly most severe to us, will be the imposition of the goods and services tax in the near future. These issues have been debated in the House already so I would like to talk about a few other issues in the time allotted to me.
There are two issues that we have not talked about, but I have had correspondence with ministers opposite trying to rectify them because of their direct effect to northerners and specifically, to single industry towns. One of those issues is Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. For those who are not familiar with this particular corporation, it has a mandate to help Canadians receive affordable housing.
CMHC has a policy concerning high-risk communities which relates specifically to mining communities in northern Ontario. Not too long ago I wrote the Minister of Housing to tell him of the particular problems this policy is creating in communities like Pickle Lake, Ignace and more than likely in the future, Red Lake and Golden. This policy does is not allow individuals in these communities, when a mine is in the process of being closed, to purchase a home without guarantees from the mine itself. There are a few problems with this. Because of northern Ontario's need to diversify its economy, it has gone to great lengths, with help from the government, to put in programs to entice businesses to move to these communities where these mines are in the process of shutting down. We come to the problem, Madam Speaker.
I have a letter from the community of Ignace and it concerns its housing shortage. Can you imagine a com-
Supply
munity sending a letter to its member of Parliament and to CMHC telling us that they have a housing shortage when, at the same time, they are telling us that a large mine is shutting down. All the houses that were built by the mine are for sale. It does not sound possible but it is a fact.
I would like like to read a few lines from this letter which outlines the situation. Ignace has a housing shortage and the letter goes on to say:
Due to industry shifts, there is a local demand for housing. The Mine has stabilized operations at 236 employees and requires all of its available housing to attract skilled personnel for the continued operation of Lyon Lake. With the closure of Camp 418 of Canadian Pacific Forest Products, between 20 and 30 employees will be looking to relocate to Ignace. Furthermore, Original Log Cabins is scheduling a spring move from Pine River, Manitoba to Ignace and will need accommodation for approximately 10 employees-
The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation General Policy on Underwriting for Ignace is destroying our potential to stabilize our economy and ultimately compromises CMHC investments made. Stable sectors within the Ignace economy are unable to secure new employees because housing is not available. This policy is encouraging Noranda and the township to walk away from housing opportunities and cease proactive economic development activities until such time as Lyon Lake closes and all the homes can be dumped on the market.
It goes on and on.
I brought this situation to the attention of the Minister of Housing not too long ago. I would like to read part of what the minister said in response. The crux of the letter, that goes on and on is this: "CMHC officials will continue to monitor the economic situation of Ignace on a regular basis to ensure that this policy does not create any hardship in the community."
I find this totally unacceptable. That is the reason why these supply days are so very important to members on this side of the House. We have particular programs and situations implemented by the Government of Canada that have affected the regions we represent. We bring them to the attention of the government and the answer is simply: "There is nothing wrong."
Let us consider the mining communities. We know that once a mine is opened eventually it will be shut. Communities are now getting more involved in trying to diversify their economies before the mine shuts down completely. As is known in mining communities, there is a cutback of employees before the magic day takes place.

May 10, 1990
Supply
Here we have a community that is working as hard as it possibly can to diversify its industry, and what do we hear from the government? It states that the policy is perfectly acceptable. Wait until the mine shuts down, and it will simply dump homes on the market. Basically, it will put the housing and real estate market right down to the lowest level where it possibly can be, and in essence, it will probably put that community and those individuals in a bankrupt position. That is totally unacceptable.
At this time, I would also like to talk a little bit about another situation that I brought to the attention of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I see that the new minister is here, which is good but even though this does not relate to him I hope he will take this very seriously.
In northern Ontario, we have many isolated reserves. The minister is very well aware of that. Not too long ago, we wrote and simply said that we must diversify the economies of those communities. In my riding, there are roughly 10,000 individuals who are isolated and have no access by road to the outside world. What takes place in those communities is that everything is flown in, except in a few key areas which have winter roads which are run on ice and very difficult to maintain.
I have written to the minister on numerous occasions and stated that I thought it was a great waste of the taxpayers' dollars to continue in the long term to fly equipment and material north to the different communities. I said that it would be to the benefit of Canada, the taxpayers and the communities themselves to look at getting involved in road building for these communities, whether they are winter roads or permanent roads.
The minister's answer is simply that government policy states that the only time they build a winter road for these reserves is when they put in funds for these roads when they have a capital project under way. I say to the minister and to Canadians who are listening that in the long run that particular policy is costing us a lot of money. If we were to look at the road system and its effects, we would see that in the long run it would be to the benefit of all taxpayers.
I see that my time is almost up. I say to the minister and the government that we have to look at these problems seriously and the effects they will have on northern Ontario and northern Canada. Because it
comes from opposition members, the government cannot just not accept them. It must look at them a little more seriously. I hope that the government will look at these two problems I have mentioned today because they are very legitimate and important concerns that we have.

Madam Speaker, I compliment the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on his speech today. He really got down to some of the specific problems that face his riding. As critic for Indian affairs and aboriginal peoples, he has been especially concerned with the problems of housing and the maintenance of reserves.
I would ask the member to comment briefly on one item in the motion before the House today that concerns the export tax on softwood lumber. There has been a general problem in northern Ontario since the imposition of the export tax on softwood lumber. That industry has become very run down.
About the same time or very shortly after the tax was imposed, the Canadian dollar rose from 73 cents or 74 cents to about 85 cents, which really imposed a second tax of 15 per cent. At the same time, regulations were brought into play which disadvantaged northern Ontario with regard to competition with British Columbia for softwood lumber sales in the United States. I know that in northeastern Ontario the combination of these three factors have had a devastating impact on that whole industry which provides a lot of employment.
It has forced a number of companies to sell out to other companies which do not necessarily have the same social and community concerns as the smaller operators had. I thought it would be useful to hear from the member about the impact on northwestern Ontario because both areas of northern Ontario are very dependent on resource industries, especially mining and forestry. I would like to know the kinds of problems faced in
May 10, 1990

northwestern Ontario with the imposition of the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber several years ago.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate that you are trying to keep us on time with our 10 minutes. I know it is always difficult to bring forward the many problems that we all have in that short time.
I thank my colleague for the question as it relates to the export tax on softwood lumber. That particular tax has created many problems for northern Ontario. Specifically, in my riding it has caused two sawmills to shut down and a third to scale down its production considerably. These are problems, as I related in my opening remarks, that will occur when we, as northerners, are given a particular policy of the government to follow, and then as members of Parliament have to try to live with that.
We have asked the government about this on numerous occasions and have been told by the Minister of Forestry that he tried to get into a negotiation type mode with the United States to look at changing this 15 per cent export tax because of the changes in the dollar and the situation that created.
Once the goods and services tax comes into effect and that 7 per cent tax is tacked on to the 15 per cent export tax, even more problems will be created because it is a long way to ship those goods to market. If that continues, we will price ourselves right out of the market.
I say to the government to be very careful when it puts those types of programs in place because of the types of situations that will occur. They will definitely affect us. To add insult to injury, there are the cuts to UI. Because of the effects of cuts in the industry, we again have to look for unemployment because there is nowhere else to work. I suggest the government has to look at all these in one context.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this motion before us today. Although it deals with all northern areas of Canada, it is of special concern and interest to those of us from northern Ontario. It covers the whole range of perceived problems we face because of government changes, both in the economy of northern Ontario and in government policy, this past couple of years.
The removal of VIA Rail service in northern Ontario, which we believe will be completely wiped out within the next couple of years, is especially distressing to communities dependent on rail service.
The tightening of the UI program is difficult for those industries that operate on a seasonal basis. The loss of the northern residents deduction for income tax purposes will be a real blow to those communities, not in the area I represent, but in the far north. We have discussed the 15 per cent export tax and the loss of the mine depletion allowance as listed here. This is a very important item.
I want to speak primarily to that item today because of the problem we face in the communities of Elliot Lake, Blind River and the north shore area of the Algoma District. During the past three months we have had the announcement that some 2,000 miners will be laid off in the next 12 months in the town of Elliot Lake with a population of 16,000, and another 5,000 in the area along the north shore, including Blind River. That is a tremendous blow. I want to deal with some of the details surrounding this lay-off and with the loss of the earned depletion allowance and flow-through shares.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources says that if we are going to have mines coming on stream in the next 10 or 12 years, whether it is in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec or other parts of our country such as Yukon or the Northwest Territories, we have to invest money now in exploration and development.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources says that we should be investing something like $1.2 billion or $1.3 billion a year now. It is not that every dollar will be successful in that regard, but if you are going to have mines coming on stream in 10 or 12 years time, you have to make the investment now. Unfortunately, in the last two or three years we have lost those major programs. We lost CEIP in the last budget. We lost the flowthrough shares and mine depletion allowance arrangements along with capital gain arrangements in the last two or three years. The result is that the amount of exploration and development dollars being spent in this industry next year will be of the order of $400 million.

May 10, 1990
Supply
That is being spent by Inco, Falconbridge and the senior mines. That means we are going to have about one-third the number of dollars being spent which our own Department of Energy, Mines and Resources say is necessary. This is extremely bad news for northern Ontario because we know that down the road, at the turn of the century, there simply will not be those new mines coming on stream. The dollars are not being spent now and under the present regime will not be spent in the years ahead. It is extremely bad news. It has to be changed. We have depended for the last five or six years on the junior mining companies, traded mostly on the Vancouver Stock Exchange, to provide the $800 million or $900 million exploration and development dollars.
The Minister of Finance has given the commitment to the Prospectors and Developers Association that he will review this matter. I know that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, if he believes his department, will want to see that happen. It is terribly urgent in the long run.
I want to talk briefly about the challenge facing us in communities like Elliot Lake, Blind River and the north shore area. Our challenge over the next 12 months and the next few years is to try to make those adjustments to maintain the viability of these communities. A lot of responsibility will fall both to the federal government and provincial governments.
The mining companies have a responsibility as well to assist in developing procedures and activities to assist their employees. I believe they have a responsibility for lump sum funds to assist mining communities in these massive capital expenditures for municipal infrastructure. I believe that should be done. A great deal of responsibility will lie with the federal, provincial and municipal governments to the extent that they are capable of doing that.
Clearly, we need money immediately for manpower mobility and job search. We face the loss of 450 jobs by August. We hope the additional loss of another 1,600 jobs will not take place until a year from now, in April or May of 1991. In fact, it may take place in August or September of this year. If that happens then the amount of money needed will be several times that being sought now by the Community Futures group.
There is a need for money for manpower mobility, job search and retraining programs. We have requested the Department of Transport and the Minister of Transport to develop and improve airport facilities. That is one alternative for the creation of employment. The idea of itinerant mining service, such as used in Rabbit Lake and Saskatoon in Saskatchewan, could be used in communities in northeastern Ontario such as Detour-du-Lac and other communities where new mines will be coming onstream.
I believe programs like the FedNor program are very beneficial in creating small expansions or development of new industry. That program is simply not adequate to deal with the massive restructuring which will have to take place in communities facing massive lay-offs. Much of this is in areas of provincial jurisdiction, so it is very important that we develop them and have programs such as ERDA and economic and regional development agreements where two levels of government can combine to put forward major industrial adjustments.
We did this a few years ago in the forest products industry where we had to restructure it to bring it up to proper environmental standards in order to create the productivity and ability to compete. That is the kind of massive industrial adjustment program we need.
I simply call on the government to be extremely co-operative and to take its responsibility seriously during the next 12 months and in the years ahead to provide industrial adjustment programs and capital intensive assistance mechanisms to ensure that communities like Elliot Lake, which are facing the loss of something like one-half to two-thirds of their labour force, can make that adjustment and continue to be viable communities, even if slightly smaller, so that their community life will continue and families will survive.
Mir. Mac Harb (Ottawa Centre): Madam Speaker, I had the honour to be in parts of northern Ontario with my colleague from Nepean on a task force that looked into infrastructures in the area. We will be reporting back to our caucus fairly soon on our findings.
One of the things that we noticed on the positive side is that northern Ontario is one of the most beautiful land masses in our country. It is one of the finest areas that
May 10, 1990

tourists can visit to look at the beauty of the rivers and lakes, as well as the mountains and valleys.
The unfortunate thing that we noticed is that there is absolutely no way that you can get to certain parts of northern Ontario because of the lack of roads, as the hon. member just mentioned.
What also astonished us was the fact that in many of those areas there are no sewage facilities. People still have to use huts.
We were informed while we were there by the mayors and reeves in the area that large numbers of youth, once they finish high school or primary level, are moving down to major cities like Toronto, Ottawa or other areas to finish their graduate studies and not returning to their homes. We are seeing a depletion in terms of the human resources that exist there.
One could suggest that this is an excellent opportunity for the government to move in and provide northerners with the tools they need, that is access to main roads. I cannot see anything wrong with the request that the government move and move fairly quickly on this issue. I would like to commend hon. members for their comments.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Ottawa Centre for his comments. One of the thrusts of municipalities in this area is the creation and improvement of transportation facilities. I have already mentioned the improvement and the requests that we have in for navigation aids to the Minister of Transport. It is urgent and important that he make a decision on that very soon.
The second area relates to road infrastructure. In the next four or five years we expect that a decision will be made by Ontario Hydro to build an electrical generating plant in the area of Dean Lake, just west of Blind River, which will involve the expenditure of some $8 billion or $10 billion over a 10-year period for an electrical generating centre.
One of the things which will be needed is a better road, transportation facilities, to that centre to accommodate workers coming from Elliot Lake and Blind River-the whole north shore area. One cannot bring in
3,000	or 4,000 construction workers and all the required infrastructure without having good transportation units
Supply
and transportation corridors. At this time we have only the Trans-Canada Highway, which is a two-lane road that will not have the needed capacity.
Co-operation between the two senior levels of government in transportation might be part of a major ERDA agreement.
The second area mentioned by the hon. member was the provision of municipal infrastructure. If we lose one-half or two-thirds of our labour force in Elliot Lake in the mining industry, which is a primary employment area, we will lose it in the area of secondary jobs as well, not to mention the service area. I think the mining companies have a responsibility to assist in the large financial obligations that the municipalities take on for municipal infrastructure for sewer and water when a mining company shuts down its operation and moves out. It seems to me it has a responsibility to provide some of the lump sum assistance in those circumstances so that the remaining population is not left with that financial obligation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I compliment the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River for presenting a motion to the House today which allows many of us, members of government and opposition, to discuss issues of concern to the north and not just to bemoan some of the problems, as they have been described, but also to talk about the tremendous positive progress that Progressive Conservative government has been making in the north since we first took office in 1984.
In fact this progress reflects a legacy of commitment to northern Canada which goes right back to the earliest times of Confederation, but it was certainly reflected in the policies of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker as Prime Minister of Canada who pioneered the roads to resources concept together with the former hon. member from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who was the minister responsible in those days and who, I might add, had as his parliamentary assistant as he travelled the north the present Prime Minister of Canada.
There is a legacy here of a sustained commitment to northern Canada by successive Progressive Conservative governments because we have always held a vision for the future of the north. That vision sees the north as a place where Canadians, those who live in the north

May 10, 1990
Supply
whether indigenous or non-indigenous, can find their future.
Other governments over the years have had the Ottawa attitude toward the north as a place to be exploited by southerners to add to the tax revenue base of the federal government, but that certainly has not been the approach that successive Progressive Conservative governments have taken.
That is why I am honoured to participate in this debate as the minister responsible not only for the needs of our Inuit and Indian people but also of all northerners, especially in the areas north of 60.
I point out that other members on the governments side, parliamentary secretaries and my colleague, the Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, will be participating in this debate. In contrast to some of the negative aspects of the motion before the House, we will be putting forward very forcefully the strong, positive record of this government in dealing with the problems of northern people.
I heard, for example, the hon. member for Algoma indicate that the motion referred to a whole range of perceived problems. I recognize that it is the role of the opposition to talk about perceived problems, to criticize, but I think we would all welcome some positive, complimentary observations on the tremendous record that this government has achieved over the past several years.
Since my appointment several weeks ago to my present responsibilities I have been travelling extensively throughout northern Canada visiting many communities, listening to and speaking with northerners and indeed making some significant progress on a number of important northern issues which I wish to describe during my comments here today.
Since 1984 there has been a dramatic positive change north of 60. I am pleased to be able to continue to assist in facilitating additional beneficial improvements.
We are changing priorities. That is why this government is not so popular at the present time. We are doing things differently for the betterment of our children and the future of Canada. We are not afraid of criticism when we know that we are doing the right things, that we
are on the right track. We are replacing old, antiquated programs and initiatives which have not worked with new improved ways of doing things to the benefit of Canadians and in the present context to the benefit of northern Canadians.
I just want to give a few indications of the progress that has been made in the period since this government was elected. It is interesting to note that incomes north of 60 in the two territories have increased by 10 per cent in the period from 1985 to 1988 in the Northwest Territories and by 30 per cent in Yukon. More significant, the Gross Domestic Product of the Northwest Territories has increased by 31 per cent over the period between 1984 and 1988. In Yukon the Gross Domestic Product has increased by 73 per cent.
These are significant indices of improvement in the Gross Domestic Product of northern communities. At a time when the economy in total has not grown nearly as rapidly we have seen a significant improvement in the economic output of those northern regions.
To reinforce those statistics, I want to point out that the commitment of the federal government since 1984 to providing assistance by way of transfer payments to the northern territorial governments has virtually doubled. When we came to office the commitment was something less than $500 million annually. It is now approaching $1 billion annually. That is a 100 per cent increase in the commitment that this government makes to the needs of northern people.
That has been reflected in a virtual doubling of the per capita assistance the federal government is rendering to the people of the north. It is being targeted, in particular, to certain areas of special need, as the mining and forestry industries change, as environmental issues take on a greater significance, and as comprehensive land claims are settled with finality for all time.
For the past three years our government's policies and programs for the north have been shaped and guided by what is called "the northern political and economic framework". It was my predecessor, now the Minister of National Defence, who took this new policy framework to cabinet, had it approved and announced it in 1987, in
May 10, 1990

order to create a consistency and a continuity to all our efforts in northern Canada, in order to develop the north more effectively in a sound and orderly fashion.
This northern political and economic framework has four main elements. The first is to continue the transfer of programs and responsibilities to the territorial governments.
The second is to settle once and for all a piece of unfinished business, that is, the comprehensive claims of northern Indian and Inuit people.
Third, this program is designed to facilitate environmentally sustainable economic development in our north by encouraging the diversification and the strengthening of northern economies.
Finally, this policy framework reinforces Canada's ability to administer effectively Arctic lands and waters, all of which adds to the strengthening of Canada's sovereignty in the north.
These are our strategic priorities for northern Canada. I am happy today to be able to report more specifically on substantial progress we have been making on a number of these fronts.
In just the past few weeks Canadians have witnessed the conclusion of final agreements with the Council of Yukon Indians and the Dene-Metis of the Western Arctic.
Just a week ago I was proud to be present in Igoolik in the eastern Arctic when we signed the agreement in principle with the Tungavik Federation of Nunavut, an agreement with the Inuit people long forgotten in terms of our obligation as a nation toward their needs, and now reflected in the signing of this important agreement in principle which will lead to a final agreement within 18 months of great benefit to the some 18,000 Inuit people of the eastern Arctic.
In the conclusion and signing of the agreement with the Council of Yukon Indians, which conveyed to the Yukon Indian people some $248 million in the form of cash settlement and 41,000 square kilometres of land in exchange for their giving up of their claims and stated rights to the balance of the Yukon Territory, we have seen the ability to bring certainty and predictability to the planning and development of the northern economic and social needs of Yukoners, both native and non-native.
That is why on April 1, on Parliament Hill, there was a great celebration upon the signing of this final agreement. The thing that I wanted to comment on is the
Supply
happiness, the joy, the sense of peace and positive optimism that accompanied the conclusion of that important agreement. After many years of negotiations, of aspiration by the Yukon Indians stretching back to 1905, this government did the right thing. We finished a piece of unfinished business which will be of tremendous benefit to that important western part of the Canadian north.
Three weeks ago we did the same thing in Yellowknife by concluding a final agreement which must now be ratified over the next few months by the Dene-Metis people. It is an agreement which involves a compensation fund of $500 million to the Dene-Metis people of the Mackenzie Valley and the western Arctic, and a
181,000	square kilometre granting of land title to the Dene-Metis people in exchange for their commitment and generosity to Canada in enabling us to complete this historic agreement.
All told, these significant agreements in northern Canada represent the final recognition of the fact that our indigenous people were here and occupied these northern lands long before the European settlers, the whalers and sailors and those who came to these shores to populate and occupy the land that we now know as Canada.
This unfinished business has been concluded by this government, bringing possible potential prosperity, stability and a very strong voice and role for northern indigenous peoples in the important political and administrative decisions to be made as we pursue orderly development of these northern parts of Canada.
That is why at all these occasions when I have met with the chiefs, elders and leaders of these communities, there has been a great sense of relief, elation and hopeful positive expectation-genuine joy-which I sensed on the part of northern people. This government and I in particular are proud to have done these fellow Canadians great justice.
These agreements in total represent a settlement amount of some $1.3 billion and the confirmation of land ownership to the Dene and Metis Indian and Inuit peoples of the north of an area almost equal to the total area of the country of France. They involve management understandings in regard to economic development in the areas of energy, forestry, mining, indigenous enterprises such as trapping, hunting and fishing, in business development, transportation and tourism promotion.

May 10, 1990
Supply
These agreements therefore all bode well for the future strength and security of northern peoples.
Since 1984, our government has also been committed to the steady transfer of provincial-type responsibilities to both Yukon and Northwest territorial governments. Our policy has been to pursue this goal, working in close co-operation with the territorial governments and at a pace with which they feel comfortable while ensuring that we continue to deliver programs in a manner fully commensurate with our existing and traditional responsibilities.
A general memorandum of understanding to guide the transfer of these programs was worked out with the government of Yukon in 1988. We expect to reach a similar understanding soon with the Northwest Territories, hopefully within the present fiscal year.
I and many of my colleagues in the federal Cabinet, including many former ministers of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, travel regularly to the northern territorial governments to meet with their leadership. In fact we continue to work in our respective jurisdictions on the orderly devolution of responsibility so that the northern territories are developing the capacity to manage their responsibilities in a sense of the full meaning of provincial status.
Good progress has been made in transferring intraterritorial highways. In fact only this week we have announced with finality the conclusion of an agreement wherein the government of the Northwest Territories will manage highways within the Northwest Territories.
I myself in my former capacity as Minister of Fisheries concluded an agreement to devolve freshwater fisheries to the Government of Yukon.
A number of other transfers are already in place and further will be negotiated and completed during the year ahead.
These will include withdrawal of my department from the land titles field in both territories and transfer of the freshwater fisheries to the Northwest Territories government. Together with Transport Canada we have recently transferred responsibility for class B and C airports in
Yukon, and we expect to make a similar transfer this year to the Northwest Territorial government.
We also are negotiating health care transfers, especially in the Yukon at the present time. We hope to revive very soon negotiations toward an agreement in principle for the transfer of forestry management responsibilities to the Government of Yukon.
All these changes that have taken place in northern Canada in the past few years have been of positive benefit. None has been more significant than the rapid political devolution of provincial-like, province-like government authorities north of 60. My department will continue to lead this process of political devolution toward the day when both territories will have the full powers and authorities comparable to those of provinces to the south.
Broadening and strengthening the economic base of our northern territories is a major challenge facing northerners, northern governments and the federal government. We are looking for improved ways to develop stable, sustainable industries that can supplement and complement the non-renewable resource industry sector.
For the past several years the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has co-operated with the territories through a series of economic development agreements and sub-agreements. Our Northern Affairs Program is the regional economic development agency for northern Canada, in some ways comparable to the Western Economic Diversification Program and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, both of which were established by this government.
Our economic development agreement with Yukon expired last year, but we are extending funding in the present year. We will be renegotiating both with Yukon and the Northwest Territories a set of new economic development agreements when the Northwest Territories' agreements expire at the end of the present fiscal year.
Future economic development programming in the north will focus on priority areas for northern people, areas such as mineral development, environmental industries, arts and crafts, tourism and community planning. The development and the assistance that we can lend will concentrate as well on remote and underdevel-
May 10, 1990

oped communities and on sustainable development opportunities relating to the northern environment.
On an international level, the recent signing of the Canada-U.S.S.R. agreement on co-operation in the Arctic represents an historic step forward in co-operation with the vast Soviet territory on the other side of Arctic pole. This agreement as you know, Madam Speaker, was signed when the Prime Minister was present in Leningrad during the month of November. It has opened a new era in Canada-Soviet Arctic collaboration. It represents a major step forward in circumpolar collaboration. I look forward to serving as a joint chairman of the Canada-U.S.S.R. mixed commission as we implement the provisions of this agreement.
In the same vein, this government committed itself to the creation of the Canadian Polar Commission which will deal with the economic and social needs of indigenous people and all northern people. We will be bringing forward the legislation creating the Canadian Polar Commission, hopefully later this year for approval and support.
We are also taking the lead in my department for developing an Arctic environmental strategy. Important consultations jointly with the Minister of the Environment and other ministers are taking place throughout Canada as part of the public discussion of "The Green Plan" of my colleague, the Minister of the Environment. Meetings will be held during the month of June with ministers present in the northern communities of Canada from Whitehorse on the west to Iqaluit in the eastern Arctic.
I think it is unfortunate that the motion put forward by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River is in a negative vein. There are many, many positive successes, achievements of this government, of all ministers working together in the spirit of previous Progressive Conservative governments and the vision of our leaders to bring true economic and social benefit, the same equality of opportunity and the quality of life to northern people that most of us enjoy here in the southern regions of Canada.
Thank you, Madam Speaker, and the hon. member for giving us an opportunity to debate these very important
Supply
questions. I am sure hon. members will be looking forward to many other positive interventions as the day unfolds from my colleagues who do, indeed, speak positively about the tremendous bright future which faces northern Canadians under Progressive Conservative government.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the minister on the agreement which has been struck concerning native land claims in parts of the far north.
I want to ask him more specifically about the land claim for the Manitoulin Island United Chiefs and Councillors land claim. On February 2 of this year an agreement was reached with First Nations of Manitoulin Island and the Ontario Government involving some 36,400 hectares of land and payment in value of $8.9 million in land claim.
During those difficult negotiations, which really reached a peak because of a court challenge by the First Nations of Manitoulin against the Province of Ontario, the federal government essentially took a position of observer status at those hearings. Yet there is a claim by the United Chiefs and Councillors, the First Nations of Manitoulin, against the federal government for the loss of the use of those lands for 128 years since the original treaties were signed in 1862.
In view of the progress that has been made on those land claims which involved right-of-way and unsold surrendered lands and so on, will the federal government's policy be similar to the agreement which was reached with the Dene and other groups in the Northwest Territories and Yukon? I am sure that eventually the federal government will end up in court with a claim by the First Nations of Manitoulin. Rather than go through all that litigation, which as sure as night follows day will occur, are the federal government and the minister willing to sit down and do the negotiations for the loss of the use of those 36,400 hectares of land during the last 128 years rather than go through the court challenge first and then be dragged kicking and screaming to the negotiation table?
Would the minister give us the general approach that he and the department would take in this specific claim for the loss of these lands over a century of time?

May 10, 1990

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Algoma for this question, which I know is extremely important to a group of his constituents, the First Nations of Manitou-lin Island.
In recent days, I have received some preliminary briefing on the status of this specific claim. I am not in a position to discuss details of any specific claim in the House. I can assure the hon. member that, in accordance with our policy on the negotiation of comprehensive and specific claims, all legal and historical factors bearing upon the federal government's position and, in this case, suggested obligation, will be examined thoroughly. We cannot resolve individual specific claims in isolation of a number factors relating to our comprehensive claims policy and the legal provisions of treaties and the extent to which they may or may not have been breached.
I certainly cannot indicate that I would personally intervene and do anything which bore a particular parallel to the comprehensive agreements which we have achieved in recent weeks, but I certainly will look seriously at the status of this claim on behalf of the hon. member for Algoma.

Through you, Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for his speech. It gives me an opportunity ask him questions that I otherwise would not have been able to.
I found the minister's speech very interesting in that he talked about much relief and elation over many of the progressive things that are happening. There are, however, some indications about the downside of northern development. Being the international year of literacy, from a Southam report and other indications, we know there is a rate of approximately 40 per cent illiteracy in the north. We have a very high drop-out rate in our schools. We also have a very high incidence of unemployment, in some areas almost as high as 90 per cent, because there are no economic development opportunities.
The minister also went on to speak about the land claims agreement signed with the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I have some very specific questions about that process.
Why did the federal government not change the comprehensive land claims policy to allow the negotiation of self-government at the same time as the negotiation of the land claims? That is a very big question for those two areas. In relation to that, does the minister believe that the inherent right to self-government should be entrenched in the Constitution?
Were there any taxation provisions made within the land claims agreement for corporations that will be developed and also for treaty Indians?
The minister also talked about a transfer of programs. It has been the experience that the transfer of programs has been severely hampered by the fact that the present level of funding for these programs is not perceived to be the same level that will be carried over along with the responsibility for those particular programs. I refer, particularly, to highways and airports.
In the Territories we have a severe problem with the standard of airport and airline safety, because we have communities that have airports that are essentially muskeg with gravel on it. That is not safe and it is not acceptable anywhere else in Canada. We rely almost solely on air transportation.
I would also like to know about the Polar Commission and his involvement in it. I know that the minister is the joint chairman of the Canada-USSR committee. Is the Polar Commission going to be a real Polar Commission? Is it going to be located in the Polar region? Is it going to be administered by Polar peoples? Is it going to be in an area that is a Polar region, or is it going to be in a central Canadian location like Ottawa or Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Western Arctic has a number of questions on her mind. Those questions are posed, I believe, in the context of general support for the initiatives that the government is taking in the western Arctic and in northern Canada.
Although the hon. member has not said so in the House, I believe that she is pleased with the conclusion of this historic agreement with the Dene-Metis people of the western Arctic. I certainly was led to believe by the hon. member that she did support the conclusion of this agreement.
May 10, 1990

There are many unanswered questions. I am not able in the time permitted me here today to answer those questions. I will be appearing before the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs next week. Other members and ministers, including my colleague, the Minister of State, will be here this afternoon and could perhaps elaborate on some of these questions.
Let me for a moment comment on this question of entrenching self-government. The comprehensive claims policy does not provide for the constitutional entrenchment of institutions of self-governments, because there has not yet been a constitutional consensus on that question at a constitutional conference attended by the premiers of the 10 provinces and the Prime Minister. With the successful conclusion of the Meech Lake Accord, which I trust the hon. member supports, we will be able to get on with dealing with those important constitutional questions, such as the definition for all time of aboriginal rights and not merely passing reference to aboriginal rights in the 1982 Constitution. It would be a true and serious discussion of the definition of entrenched self-government. Those are constitutional matters.
I am sure the hon. member and all members of the House want us to conclude this historic Meech Lake agreement with the Province of Quebec so that we can get on with making these important further steps of constitutional improvement on behalf of the aboriginal people of Canada.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate today. I compliment the member for Kenora- Rainy River for having given us this opportunity to discuss in the House issues and problems facing northern Canada. I would also like to say that I appreciated the comments of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Certainly, I do not want to give the impression that we live in a totally black and white world, and that there is not from time to time progress made on some fronts. However, the Minister drew attention to the fact that the government represents the tradition of the late John George Diefenbaker and his vision for northern Canada. I must say to him that I represent the constituency that the late John Diefenbaker represented and certainly the residents of that constituency do not feel that there is
Supply
the same type of commitment to northern development as this government's predecessors made so evident.
The minister dealt with some of the accomplishments of the government and the issues facing the Territories and the far northern regions of the country. But very often the areas that tend to be forgotten are the northern areas of the provinces. Very often, those are regions that are both out of sight and out of mind to both the provincial and federal governments. It is that type of region that I represent and that type of region that I would like to speak to in my remarks today.
Life has never been easy in many of these communities. They obviously face some of the most rigorous climates in the country. They have always suffered from isolation. There have often been boom-and-bust cycles going all the way back to the fur trade, then through the mining industry, the forestry industry, and the other industries that have grown up in the isolated areas of the country.
Very often these communities have felt, and rightly so, that they were victims of decisions made elsewhere, that the levers of power were not in their hands, and that, in fact, both politically and economically, they were very far from being able to control their own destiny, much more so than communities in southern Canada.
This whole phenomena of being left out of the decision-making process and the feeling of powerlessness has been accentuated and reinforced by the philosophy of the government, for which it makes no apologies. It is very much a bottom-line philosophy which says that big business can set the agenda for the country. Essentially, if something is in the interest of big business, if it serves the needs of the free flow of international capital, it is the government's job and responsibility essentially to get out of the way of any type of control over what happens to the big capital and the big dollar, and to leave the decisions affecting these communities to board-rooms-not necessarily even in the big metropolitan centres of our own country, but centres in the United States, Europe, Japan and other places.
Certainly, the free trade agreement moves us another step down that road. A whole shameful phenomenon of the government arguing that it needs to bring some fiscal sense to the country so that we do not perpetually pay such a high percentage of our tax dollar in interest charges is a legitimate argument. Nevertheless, the

May 10, 1990
Supply
government has repeatedly seen fit to make cuts to those who are the most vulnerable, who have the least ability to fight back, who are not going to be heard when the cuts happen them and whose protests often go ignored.
An example of this is the regional development programs. In western Canada, last year 16 agreements expired worth $310 million. This year another 10 regional development agreements expired worth $316 million. In Saskatchewan, alone, these agreements were worth $190 million.
The people of my constituency and I feel that in a particularly direct fashion because we have calculated that these agreements-the forestry agreement; the tourism agreement; the mineral development agreement; and the NEDSA agreement (the Northern Economic Development Subsidiary Agreement) in Saskatchewan-meant approximately 1,500 jobs every year in my constituency. This constituency has a very high unemployment rate and a rapidly growing labour force. Yet, this government has seen fit to go a whole year playing internal bureaucratic games trying to figure out who is responsible for regional development, be it sectoral ministers or regional development ministers. This constituency has been left high and dry for a whole year while 1,500 jobs were lost.
In the meantime, many valuable initiatives in forestry, tourism, and, particularly, community development in areas like the Clearwater region, northeast Saskatchewan, the La Ronge region and others, have been left to die on the vine. These were initiatives that people thought were going to continue.
We have seen huge cuts to the fur industry. We have seen cuts to the Native Communications Program. Missi-nipi Broadcasting, one of the prime vehicles of communication in northern Saskatchewan, had to go off the air for the whole month of April because of the budget cut that it experienced. The very valuable publications, Saskatchewan Indian and New Breed were also cut.
We have seen the whole gutting of the UI program. The UI program was never a particularly successful program in northern Canada for a number of reasons. First, it is very difficult to establish an unemployment rate through the mechanisms used by Statistics Canada.
Certainly, in the La Ronge region, which is the northern region of Saskatchewan, there is an official unemployment rate of 13 per cent to 15 per cent. That is hardly credible because the majority of those communities are experiencing unemployment rates of 50 per cent or 60 per cent, or even higher than that. Then we see an unemployment insurance program being brought in that is predicted by the government to cost this region of the country $4 million. However, by other estimates, it will cost $11 million in lost benefits, not taking into account the seasonal nature of employment. It will make it even more difficult for people to try to patch together a living from the different kinds of opportunities that come to them from time to time so they can remain living in their communities and take advantage of the opportunities that do offer themselves. The changes to the UI program are going to make that even more difficult.
The Northern Tax Benefit Program is now very much called into question by a task force which this government appointed. I might add, the task force was appointed before the election which raised people's expectations that all isolated communities that should be eligible for this program would be eligible for it. After the election, it recommended that of the 3,224 communities that were originally eligible for this particular benefit, only 423 be left eligible. In Saskatchewan, only 15 out of the 165 communities that were previously eligible for the northern tax benefit would remain eligible under these recommendations. This is totally unacceptable. Not only is the cost of living so much higher in these regions, as everybody knows, but it makes it even more difficult to develop a viable society, a society that has professionals, business people and people who are able to carry on the tasks that a modem economy in those regions requires.
We have seen cuts in the flow-through share program. In Flin Flon, Manitoba, there is a smelter that desperately needs upgrading to meet today's environmental standards, yet the financing for that smelter depends very much on new mineral deposits being found. The way those mineral deposits are going to be found is if the junior exploration companies, which are very dependent on these flow-through shares, are able to stay in business and continue their activities.
May 10, 1990

We have also seen the introduction of the goods and services tax. Again, we see this having a particularly negative impact on northern areas. In northern areas, the costs of many goods and services are sometimes as much as two or three times as high as in comparable southern communities, and incomes are certainly no higher. This will mean that the impact of the goods and services tax is felt by the region of the country which is least able to afford it. Given the high illiteracy rate and the fact that many people still rely on the traditional economy and are not registered under the income tax system, the tax credit, which the government claims is going to mitigate the impact of the goods and services tax, will not be available to many of these people.
We also see a desperate need for housing. Housing conditions in many communities are desperately overcrowded, contributing to family breakdown, to poor performance of children in schools, and to a sense that these communities are not able to enjoy the same standard of living and the same type of amenities that lead to a healthy and productive life.
What do we see from this government? On the one hand, we see a cut-back, and on the other hand, a study. Certainly, neither a cut-back nor a study will solve the problems of housing.
In closing, I would like to offer a few suggestions that I think the government should look at seriously. We need to look at the whole situation of northern development, not just in terms of business development, not just in terms of assisting business, but look at economic development as a whole. We need to take a comprehensive look at what it takes to develop a modem economy in the communities of northern Canada, with a focus on community development, some faith and assistance for the grassroots, and some assistance to build the kind of infrastructure that we need.
We need sectoral organizations that can organize the producers in the various renewable resource sectors. We need to require the banks to give some kind of banking service to the northern communities, because it is virtually impossible to run any kind of economy without access to a banking system. We also need a modern transportation and communications system.
Supply
We have to take our commitment to sustainable development seriously. If there is any one development that is going to assist the communities of northern Canada towards a brighter future, it is if southern Canadians and Canadians as a whole take the whole concept of sustainable development seriously. Two-thirds of the country lies within what is often referred to as northern Canada.
There should be community based monitoring of resources and the setting aside of 12 per cent of our land area, as the member for Skeena recommended, to make sure that we look after it. Not only will those areas be protected for the good of the ecosystem, but also so that people from around the world will see this as a place to visit and tourism will be enhanced. We should also make sure that we do not see continuing conflict between economic development and the environment.
All of these things depend very much on us taking sustainable development seriously and making sure that the communities in the north are an integral part of this development. It is their environment, after all, an environment many of them have lived in for thousands of years.
Without serious and significant movement towards native self-government and the settlement of native land claims, we are not going to see the type of development in northern Canada which all of us would want to see.
The largest growing sector of the population in this country is the native population and much of the native population of this country resides in northern communities.
The frustration is growing. Institutions need to develop to capitalize on the type of momentum and aspirations which have been developing in the native community over the last number of years, as well as the confidence that has been developing in their own institutions. Without a serious commitment to that whole evolution, the development of northern Canada is going nowhere.
The minister made reference to the fact that we need to pass the Meech Lake Agreement so that development toward self-government can occur. I would like to say to

May 10, 1990
Supply
the minister that the time is long overdue to recognize the whole thrust towards native self-government and the role of aboriginal people in this country.
Northerners have worked as hard as any Canadians to build this country. Northerners have the same hopes and aspirations for themselves and their communities as any other Canadians do. Northerners demand and deserve the same respect and sensitivity from their government as any Canadians do.
Therefore, I call on the government to see the world through the eyes of northerners, to stop letting its philosophy get in the way of what really needs doing in northern Canada, and help northerners make the contribution to the building of the Canada of the future that they want to make and which they can make.

Madam Speaker, I would like to remind my hon. colleague from Prince Albert-Churchill River that for some time, we have often heard members of his party speak in this House against flow-through shares because they claimed these shares were tax breaks or benefits for the wealthy and rich in society.
I well understand his interest in seeing an industry in his constituency develop, and mining exploration is important for that industry, but I am surprised to see him today ask the government to use tax incentives to encourage mining exploration and development when a while ago, he and some of his fellow members spoke against flow-through shares; they used opposition days to speak against them.
My other point, as a supplementary question, Madam Speaker, is to ask him to admit with me that in recent months, this government has made considerable efforts with the native peoples, the first nations, for self-government, and I would ask him to acknowledge that with me.

I thank the member for his question. I was elected to this House in the fall of 1988. Therefore, I was not party to the debate with respect to flow-through shares before that time.
I do understand that this was an aspect of fiscal policy that my party did support in principle. Their opposition to particular aspects of it came with details of the
program that perhaps did permit tax advantages to accrue that in some cases may not have been warranted.
I would like to point out to the member, as perhaps he knows, that $3 billion of the $4.8 billion of mineral investment that occurred through the flow-through share program was spent by junior mining companies, not the major companies. Therefore, I think it is entirely consistent because these junior mining companies are the ones that create the most local employment and are very often headquartered in the northern communities rather than in the metropolitan areas of the country. Therefore, I do not think that it is an inconsistent position on the part of my party at all.
His second question dealt with the whole aspect of self-government and land claims. In my own constituency there are two outstanding claims. One that has been recognized is the claim by the Peter Ballantyne Band which is a huge land claim. The economic development of the whole northeast part of Saskatchewan depends very much on that claim being resolved.
Another land claim which has not been recognized but is being pressed by the La Ronge Indian Band has resulted in caveats being applied in the Candle Lake area of Saskatchewan. The band is using that mechanism to try and attract the attention of the government to something they have been pressing for for about 15 years. It has not got the attention of the government. Certainly it has the attention of the property holders in the region whose properties now have caveats attached to them. From the perspective of the Indian people of my constituency, they do not see movement toward self-government. They have not seen any kind of constitutional movement since the breakdown of the First Ministers' Conferences some years ago. If there is to be such a movement, certainly people would welcome it.
I would like to give credit to the appointment of a treaty commissioner in Saskatchewan. I do want to recognize that as something that has been welcome and I welcome it myself.

Madam Speaker, I was listening to the hon. member for Prince AJbert-Churchill River talking about the need for co-operation between the two levels of government. It struck me that a lot of the agreements which took place in past years are ending up the same way as this year's whole fiasco on financial support to western farmers.
May 10, 1990

The government waited for three or four months after the demand by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the premier of the province for special funding, finally called in the provincial ministers and negotiated for a couple of days towards the end of March, getting very close to the start of the seeding period, and finally placed $500 million on the table but demanded that there be support from the provinces.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance brought in a budget which cut the transfer payments by $100 million or $200 million to these provinces, placing them in a financial position where they could not possibly match the federal government funding. One minister said: "Well, we really snookered those guys this time because they have not got the money to put up to match it". All the while, farmers are at a loss to get the funds that they need for seeding their crops this spring.
This morning, we see a headline in The Financial Post which states: "Prairie premiers won't match federal farm aid". It goes on to say that there is a common front by the western premiers. I wonder if the hon. member sees this as a technique to make the government look good, as it is attempting to do, while the provinces cannot possibly come up with their share of the money. All this time, the farmers are suffering. They do not have any money.

Mr. Speaker, certainly I can identify with the comments of the hon. member for Algoma. Not only do I represent northerners, but I represent farmers who are becoming very frustrated with this whole game of political arm wrestling that has been going on.
Indeed, I can also identify with the point he makes that the cuts in transfer payments to the provinces have a severe impact on northern areas of the country because those are under-serviced areas generally. Cuts in transfer payments means that the under-servicing will continue.
With respect to regional development programs, the government does not even look good. With respect to the farmers, the whole game perhaps is to make the government look good while, at the same time, not spending any money. This whole situation has to come to
Supply
a quick head because the small wonder is that the government is running 15 per cent in the public opinion polls. While this may make for good headlines and satisfy hon. members opposite in the House, the farm community and the northerners who are falling victim are not going to put up with this kind of thing much longer.
