speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have some comments on the answer given by the hon. member who spoke for the New Democratic Party to the question asked by the Liberal member for Algoma concerning transfer payments and federal-provincial agreements that were steadily diminishing. I would also appreciate the hon. member's comments on the fact that from 1984 to 1988, the federal government, with the provinces, invested over $1.1 billion in forestry agreements, and that in 1988, after the election, the federal government renewed agreements with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and signed a Plan de I'Est with Quebec. Unlike the Liberals and the New Democrats, the federal government does not act unilaterally but prefers to negotiate with the provinces.
I may remind the hon. member, when he speaks about forestry and agriculture, that the provinces have at least as much responsibility as the federal government in this area and that the problems facing farmers can only be dealt with through co-operation, consultation and concrete funding.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Time for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Western Arctic.

Madam Speaker, I would very much like to take this opportunity to talk about a vibrant and enthusiastic part of Canada where we believe we can make a significant contribution to this great country, Canada.
Together, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories make up over one third of Canada. As you know, Madam Speaker, it is a land of startling beauty and diverse geography. Fewer than 80,000 people live in approxi-

May 10, 1990
Supply
mately 75 communities scattered over this vast part of Canada.
In the Northwest Territories, one third of the people are Dene and Metis, one third are Inuit and one third are non-native. All Dene and Metis communities are located inland along the major river and lake systems in the forested western portion of the territories. All Inuit communities are coastal, except for Baker Lake.
For thousands of years, native people in the Canadian Arctic lived a subsistence lifestyle depending upon fish and wildlife to provide food, clothing, tools and materials for shelter. As fur traders, miners and whalers moved north, life for native people began to change. Although adjustments to lifestyle continue, even today the primary foods for most northern Dene, Metis and Inuit families are still fish from the lakes, rivers and oceans, and meat from caribou, moose, seal, musk-ox and water fowl. Good hunting and fishing skills are respected by everyone and often influence the choice of a community leader. These are not just recreational items or activities. If it sounds like I am describing something which sounds unfamiliar, I probably am. Most Canadians have not been there but Canada's Arctic is what makes Canada unique.
With regard to Meech Lake, my constituents will know that as a member of the special committee to study Premier McKenna's proposed resolution, I am working diligently with my colleagues to ensure that northerners are not casualties of the 1987 Meech Lake Accord.
I want to express appreciation on behalf of Western Arctic residents to Premier McKenna of New Brunswick. His proposal stands in stark contrast to those who have treated the negative impact on the north as an acceptable level of damage in this round. When our Minister of Justice, Michael Ballantine, appeared before the special committee, he stated and I quote: "Premier McKenna has given us hope that our efforts to improve upon the Meech Lake Accord over the past three years have not been in vain."
Northerners complained about the alteration of the process for the creation of new provinces. The extension of provincial boundaries, the lack of territorial participation in the nomination of senators and Supreme Court judges and the exclusion of the territories from the whole consultative process leading to the Meech Lake
Accord are many of the concerns that the New Brunswick resolution addresses.
The Prime Minister failed to represent the northerners when we were excluded from the meeting in May 1987 and he has neglected to show any principle or fair leadership since. He did not recognize that, like Quebecers, northerners are eager to become full partners in the constitutional councils of this nation. The Prime Minister is wrong if he believes that Quebec wanted the two territories to become casualties in this national reconciliation with Quebec. The Northwest Territories is the only jurisdiction in Canada in which aboriginal peoples constitute a majority of the population. The elected representatives of the people of the Northwest Territories are trying to shape a tolerant society that will meet the distinct aspirations of Canadians in the northern third of Canada.
I am pleased to tell the members of this House that through a recent amendment to the NWT Official Languages Act, the legislative assembly has recognized the six major aboriginal languages as official languages of the Northwest Territories along with English and French. This is unique in Canada. In many ways northerners are showing leadership in their desire to try to understand one another. They are role models for all Canadians. There are 53 distinct and unique aboriginal languages indigenous to Canada, only three of which are not threatened and there are no provisions for these languages anywhere. Aboriginal peoples in the Northwest Territories have been striving to be full partners in Canada for a very long time. Recently, the Dene-Metis and Inuit initialled comprehensive claims packages which cover most of the territories. Now that outstanding comprehensive land claims in the north are finally being concluded, the people of the Northwest Territories are in a much better position to move toward provincial status in a way that respects the place of the distinct aboriginal cultures of the north.
Northerners goals for provincehood is also enhanced by the north's rich resources. Oil and gas reserves in the north could make Canada energy self-sufficient. The Government of the Northwest Territories is negotiating with the federal government a northern energy accord which would give the N.W.T. control and management of oil and gas rights, including the administration of oil and gas resource revenues such as royalties, bonus payments, rentals and licence fees. If the federal government would give Canadians some indication of its national energy
May 10, 1990

policy, then northerners and westerners could plan with more certainty the development of oil and gas resources. But we do not know whether the government is committed to frontier energy or east coast or tar sands.
In typical fashion, the government continues to play one region against the other. The federal government has to start recognizing what northern Canada can offer instead of trying to cripple our very existence. Government members must wake up to the fact that the nineties are here.
For decades, the Northwest Territories has been described as the last frontier, a part of this nation having great potential, but not yet fully integrated into the Canadian mainstream. I have tried to challenge this myth since I was elected to Parliament, but challenging the myths and perception about the frontier also means identifying how we could be affected, like any other region of this country, by forces which are sometimes beyond our control.
This means identifying how national initiatives, such as the GST, could undermine the encouraging economic climate we are currently experiencing and which is expected to continue into the future. In its current form, the introduction of the GST will mean that northerners will pay more taxes on almost all purchases. In total they will pay much more than residents of southern Canada who purchase similar baskets of goods and services.
An employee in the Northwest Territories earning $30,000 might have the purchasing power of an individual earning $20,000 in the south. The southern resident will receive the full benefit of a tax credit, but the northern resident will not because the credit will be phased out for families earning over $24,800 annually. The impact of the GST on business and industry in the north is disastrous.
I do not know if the economy of the north is strong enough to withstand another two or three years of the federal government's anti-regional development policies. The 59 communities scattered throughout the N.W.T. are located in an area comprising roughly one third of Canada's land mass and only six of them are
Supply
accessible on a year-round basis by the national road network.
Forty per cent of the population must rely entirely on air and marine transportation services for the movement of people and goods. Referring to the minister's speech, through you Madam Speaker, it has to be a consideration when these programs are developed or transferred. The distances between these communities are great and, combined with the small population in most of them, the result is that the costs of getting into and out of them are high, compared to southern Canada.
Employers are forced to maintain expensive stockpiles of materials and equipment to ensure continued operations. These conditions, coupled with the possibility of delayed access due to extreme weather, restrict the mobility of a large number of N.W.T. residents, limiting not only access to goods and services but also access to training and job opportunities.
The housing shortage is also critical in the Northwest Territories. The need and demand for public housing and subsidized home ownership is growing, far exceeding the supply available. Physical and systemic barriers to employment also exist. The lack of readily available day care facilities, adult training centres and public housing rental rate structures create disincentives to those on welfare and must be overcome. We have waited for six years for this government's child care program, but the Prime Minister cannot understand that six years is too long.
I would like to thank you for this opportunity. The north is a diverse region of this country. We have many aspects of our economy, of our constitutional development, of our social entity that we could speak to and go on forever, but I know my time is limited.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague on a very good speech in the House of Commons as it relates to the difficulties of the far north.
I would like to ask my colleague a specific question relating to her remarks about Meech Lake. I would like to know her feelings and the feelings of people in the north relating to the creation of provinces, if Meech Lake goes through as is. I think that is something I have heard her speak of on numerous occasions. It would be

May 10, 1990
Supply
to the benefit of all of us to have her elaborate on that particular difficulty as it relates to that agreement.

Madam Speaker, it is not so much what I as a member of Parliament feel but what my constituents and government representatives of the Northwest Territories have put forward to the joint standing committee of the Senate and the committee on which I sit to deal with the McKenna resolution.
The Northwest Territories want to revert to the pre-1982 arrangement for the creation of provinces, that is for the government to have the sole jurisdiction for the creation of provinces, which is how all the other provinces were created. This is what they want. This is what McKenna's recommendation is and what seems to be favourable. They feel anything outside that will freeze them out forever and negate any opportunity for them to become provinces in the future.

Madam Speaker, I have a short question for my hon. colleague. I too congratulate her on her presentation.
Based on her intimate knowledge of the north and the Dene people, I would like to ask a specific question regarding the Dene-Metis agreement signed recently. I have heard that the Dene people are very supportive of it. We have heard some positive comments, but I have not heard the member give her official position on it. I would appreciate her taking advantage of this opportunity to give us her position on the recent signed agreement.

Madam Speaker, I have absolutely no hesitation in making my position clear. I spoke with the Dene-Metis, before they set forth to initial the agreement, on my views regarding the agreement. I sat in the House when the Prime Minister indicated that he wanted me to thank the government for the Dene-Metis having initialled such a wonderful agreement.
My own official position is that the Dene-Metis have worked very hard for the last 16-odd years. I congratulate them because they had to go through a very difficult negotiation process. That process involved their affinity for the land, their lifestyle and the fact that they settled the land claims without dealing with one or two very crucial elements.
The Dene-Metis wanted to negotiate self-government while negotiating land claims, but because the land claims comprehensive policy was as it was and the government would not change it, they could not do that. Furthermore, the minister indicated there could not be the possibility of entrenching self-government in the Constitution until the first ministers were on board at a constitutional conference.
It has been a severe dilemma for the aboriginal peoples who have settled land claims not to have self-government. I have indicated to my people that they make the decisions and I support them whole-heartedly.

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak today on the motion of my colleague who represents the riding of Kenora-Rainy River. I am pleased to speak on this motion because I think the government has to hear what the people are saying regarding its policies. That is exactly what I will try to do today.
The government's record with regard to the well-being of the northern region is shameful. As a member of Parliament representing a northern Ontario riding I am very concerned about the effects of recent legislation introduced by the government.
I am speaking more specifically about the Unemployment Insurance Act, Bill C-21, the VIA Rail cut-backs, and the effects of the goods and services tax especially as it relates to tourism in northern Ontario.
The proposed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act will have an extremely negative impact on the poor and middle class in my riding of Nipissing as well as on the rest of the country and northern Ontario. It will also put a heavy burden on small business which makes up the majority of the economy in the north.
The government has targeted the average person and small business with a whopping new federal tax, one that it is now trying to sell to the public. How will the government ensure that the social safety nets are in place to protect people who bear the burden of unemployment this new tax will likely create? The government hits people with another blow, another unemployment insurance cut when they are already down.
At a time of expected inflation, economic slowdown and therefore anticipated unemployment, a responsible
May 10, 1990

government should be trying to ensure that its social safety nets are secure and something in which the people can have a sacred trust.
How does this government plan for the future of its citizens? It has done so through the eyes of the free traders who want to make sure that the government makes no contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. This government is proposing to stop contributing to the fund completely.
Its cutting of contributions will be substantial, about $2.9 billion this year, and it will leave the workers and business to pick up the shortfall. This will mean an increase in contributions by workers and employers. For small business which makes up the majority of the northern Ontario economy, it will put pressure on them when it comes time to expand. Can they really afford to hire anyone else? Can they afford the ever increasing rates of contributions.
We all know that those increased costs are passed on to the consumers whose net pay has just decreased through the higher deduction for unemployment insurance. This government's quest for a level playing field is going to end up ploughing under the workers and small businesses in northern Ontario.
The tourist industry which northern Ontario relies on cannot withstand more cost increases. We are already seeing the impact of this government's policy in this sector. The tourist industry is a large employer in the north. How will the workers survive on the reduced benefits that they must rely on with seasonal jobs?
The government looked at the unemployment insurance fund and saw a surplus last year. With its usual lack of foresight, instead of realizing that a surplus is necessary during economic growth so that funds will be there during a recession, it decided it was great time to pull out of the program altogether.
The government saw the surplus as a perfect excuse to walk away from its responsibility to the unemployed in this country. It could not leave it at just that. It would have been bad enough, but it was not enough for this government. No, it also had to increase the number of weeks needed to be eligible for benefits and then cut the length of time a person can collect.
In my riding of Nipissing a person would need 17 weeks of employment to receive about 24 weeks of
Supply
benefits if the legislation were in effect today. Even if a person has never collected before in his or her life, he or she is only eligible for 45 weeks of benefits. If the government is no longer going to give money to this program, then why on earth should it be deciding by itself how to change the program? Where is the input from employers and employees? Who will pay for the entire program?
Employers know that without unemployment insurance the local economy suffers. They know that people on unemployment insurance can at least afford to keep buying essentials and paying their bills. That will not be the case if they are forced on to welfare.
Tourism is one of the biggest hidden industries in the country, particularly in northern Ontario. It is an industry which contributes $24 billion to Canada's Gross National Product, which provides employment for 10 per cent of the country's workforce, and which is Canada's second largest earner of foreign exchange at $7 billion per year. It provides employment in all regions of Canada including summer employment for students and part-time employment and jobs for unskilled labour.
In the near north alone tourism generates $200 million annually and $1 billion across northern Ontario, yet through its policies the government continues to neglect this vital industry and places its existence in jeopardy.
In 1989 we experienced the unprecedented $3 billion balance of payments deficit in the travel account. To compound the problem, Canada's share of world tourism has been cut in half over the last decade. What is the government doing? It is making it even more difficult for our industry to compete effectively by adding an additional cost of at least 7 per cent.
Fifty per cent of travel in Canada as a whole and seventy-five per cent of travel in northern Ontario is a result of Canadians deciding to travel. Where is the incentive for our own citizens to travel in our own country when they can get more value for their money south of the border? With the exception of British Columbia, every province has experienced a net decline in tourism over the past year.
With the dismantling of defence industries around the world and the opening of the East Bloc tourism in the 1990s will rapidly become the world's largest industry. With its natural endowments and breathtaking scenery Canada is in an excellent position to expand its market

May 10, 1990
Supply
share. This could only happen if we offer good value at competitive prices and if we undertake more effective promotion. However tourism is highly price sensitive. There is no question that if the GST is introduced it will cripple this industry. What about more effective promotion, when the government slashes the budget for tourism from $35 million to $20 million at the same time as it provides about $30 million in aid to McDonnell-Douglas of Toronto? One has to question the priorities of the government.
Let us examine the effect of the GST on northern development. Northerners experience high prices for most consumer goods, and industries in the north incur higher costs due to higher transportation costs. With a 7 per cent GST added to transportation, how enticing does the government think it will be for business to set up shop in the north?
The cut-backs to VIA Rail are yet another example. Last year's cuts to VIA rail were a tremendous blow to the northern Ontario region. Thousands of VIA Rail workers lost their jobs and the effects on the economy were crippling. Transportation infrastructure in the north is absolutely essential for the development of its economy. How are northern towns and cities supposed to attract industries and tourists if we further reduce the transportation infrastructure?
The government advocates economic policies that are almost entirely based on the private sector as the driving force of the economy. We have news for the government: the economy in northern Ontario is suffering, and it does not need a kick in the vicinity especially where your back changes it name. That is what this government has done.
Traditionally Canada has always maintained a balance between the private and the pubic sector to keep its economy strong and vibrant. This principle is especially important in the poorer regions of Canada which are dependent on the government for their economic wellbeing.
Canada's northern region is no exception to that. Northern Ontario needs the implication of the government to develop itself to its full potential. A good transportation system is essential to achieve that. I urge
the government to reintroduce the VIA Rail routes which were cut and to reaffirm its commitment to the north. It is clear to all of us on this side of the House and to all the people of the north that the present policies of this government are extremely devastating to the north.
Why is this government not listening to the people who elected it? These people are asking the government to put policies in place which will assist them, but the government is proposing and advocating detrimental policies.
We need the VIA Rail service for a proper transportation infrastructure. We need a proper unemployment insurance system which will assist economic development in the north. We do not want the GST; it will only cause considerable hardship to our economy.
Finally, we want a strong commitment from this government for the well-being of the north. I do not think I can make myself clearer on these issues. I just hope that this message has been clearly understood by our present government. I thank you, Madam Speaker, and my colleague from northern Ontario for the opportunity to speak on this motion.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Nipissing, on his very extensive and detailed analysis of what is going on in the north. Particularly, as I think all my hon. colleagues will know, I feel very strongly about his words relative to VIA Rail. It is nice to see the parliamentary secretary here today to listen to these remarks about VIA Rail. I hope the government will heed the words of the hon. member.
One of the areas the member did not touch on which is something that is also very critical to northerners is the high interest rates and how they affect northern business. I thought it might be appropriate to ask the hon. member to elaborate and give us some insight on what the effects of high interest rates will be on northerners if these rates stay at the current level or increase in the coming months.

have bogged down mainly because of the current high interest. The companies that are looking to come to northern Ontario are holding back and waiting for the interest rates to go down. Nipissing is probably one of the more active communities in northern Ontario in enticing business to come to that area. We have been fairly successful in utilizing a lot of the government programs and have been very successful in enticing new business to the North Bay and Nipissing areas. A lot of companies that want to come to northern Ontario are looking at expansion but are waiting out the interest rates and that is having a tremendously detrimentalaffect in northern Ontario.
The Canadian dollar is high and I think that the people who want to compete in the United States, now that the free trade agreement is here-we might not like it but we have to live with it-are waiting for the dollar to drop so they can compete under the free trade agreement and make money. We have lots of money but who can afford to borrow at the present rates?
The regional development program of the government seems to make it easier to move different departments in the area than to develop. We have many opportunities for development but with the high interest rates it is very difficult. In northern Ontario we would certainly appreciate the interest rates dropping so that we could become competitive with the rest of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I too, appreciate the comments from my hon. colleague opposite. I would like to put my question with regard to his comments on VIA Rail.
The number one problem in this country, I am told regularly by my constituents, is the state of the national deficit. They are concerned about spending. We all know that the average subsidy for every rider on VIA Rail was about $100 last year. We were spending over $600 million a year subsidizing VIA Rail. It is very comfortable sitting in the opposition criticizing the cut-backs in VIA Rail. I would like to know how much more the hon. member
Supply
was willing to subsidize VIA Rail before he would support a cut-back in the service.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question. The VIA Rail cut-backs were devastating to northern Ontario and I think that although the people on this side of the House recognize the deficit, to cut off a service that is of really great help to northern Ontario is not the way to go about it, especially the way the government did.
It does have VIA Rail running through northern Ontario but, for some reason, it has it running through the northern portion of the province which has a population draw of roughly 50,000 to 60,000 people, instead of maintaining a route through North Bay, Sudbury and the Thunder Bay area which has a draw of roughly 400,000 people.
If the government is trying to provide a service to northern Ontario that would help expansion that, in my mind, is not the way to do it. The particular run that through northern Ontario that it cut was the third most efficient run of VIA Rail. According to some of the articles in the paper recently, VIA Rail was on track. According to many reports, it was just a matter of time before many of these runs that were cut would have become viable.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to debate today the motion put forward by the hon. member for Keno-ra-Rainy River, who also is in regular attendance at the transport committee meetings. I am sure his seatmate was speaking about something dear to his heart. This government is committed to building a strong economy encouraged by incentive and opportunity, an economy which is competitive with the world's trading nations.
In order to fully achieve this goal we must create a solid base which will allow our economy to flourish in the coming years. Measures which seek to control the deficit and reduce the national debt are an essential element to this foundation for the future.
Equally, measures which seek to establish a sound fiscal framework to sustain continued economic development are essential to our purpose. These objectives are reflected in this government's commitment to a sound transportation policy. Transportation is and always will be at the heart of our nation's economy. This is why we

May 10, 1990
Supply
have undertaken to provide Canadians with a safe and efficient transportation sector. This commitment is the core upon which our policy of economic regulation reform was built.
Madam Speaker, I should indicate to you I will be sharing my time with the hon. member for Abitibi.
With the advent of the free trade agreement the role played by transportation in our economic development has become increasingly vital as we enter the next decade and the next century. A cost-effective transportation system is essential if Canada is to preserve and enhance its position in world trade. In order to meet this challenge we must make the best of each mode of transportation. We are not just talking about air, rail, marine, truck, and bus transportation, but the use of the automobile as a transportation mode, something with which Canadians have a love affair.
Continued subsidization of a mode of transportation which costs more and more and used less and less is not a sound investment in our future, particularly when that investment is being made with the Canadian taxpayers' money. That was exactly the situation we were facing with respect to our national rail passenger network.
VIA Rail subsidy rose to an unprecedented $641 million in 1988. This translates into a subsidy of $100 per passenger. We were asking all Canadians to pay this subsidy but only 3 per cent of the travelling public used this mode of transportation. Canadians have demonstrated their preference for other modes of transportation. With a market share of 84 per cent, the automobile is clearly the mode of choice.
Reducing the subsidies to VIA Rail was a difficult decision to make. We had a system that was expensive and inefficient. The government, however, does recognize that in a country as large and diverse as ours there are some truly isolated communities which do not have access to any other mode of transportation. In order to meet this need, nine routes in five provinces were maintained and continue to be subsidized. They are Winnipeg to Capreol, which can now be serviced by The Transcontinental; Jasper to Prince Rupert; The Pas to Lynn Lake; Wabowden to Churchill; Winnipeg to Churchill; Sudbury to White River; Montreal to Senneterre; Senneterre to Cochrane; and Montreal to Jonquiere.
Many other countries are making decisions concerning rail passenger services based on their unique demographic and economic realities. Our decision has to be considered in light of the fact that we have the second largest country in the world with one of the smallest populations. VIA service must be consistent with the realities of the density of the Quebec-Windsor corridor and also the different needs of Canada's regions.
Contrary to the wording of the motion before us today, I believe we have taken the necessary action to ensure the future of VIA as a national, affordable and sustainable rail passenger network. The combined public and private spending on transportation in Canada over the next 10 years can only be measured in hundreds of billions of dollars. Therefore, an effective consideration of such an integrated system required the government to establish a forum that would permit all Canadians to be heard in a thoughtful, comprehensive and forward looking manner.
The royal commission announced by the Prime Minister at the same time as the changes to VIA Rail, will inquire into and report on a national integrated inter-city passenger transportation system to meet the needs of Canada and Canadians well into the future.
The size and importance of our transportation system cannot be overstated. Its future development must lead to a system which will meet the challenges of the 21st century.
The royal commission was asked to inquire into and recommend solutions on the role of a national integrated inter-city passenger transportation system and its relationship to the entire transportation system, the structure of a suitable multi-modal transportation system demonstrating linkages, the potential for and constraints on achieving a national system and the appropriate financial arrangements to achieve such a system, taking into account the jurisdiction of all levels of government and the role of the private sector.
The commission will look ahead into the 21st century to advise the government on the needs of Canadians and on the relationship between the modes of transportation of the future. This royal commission, through its wide consultation and broad mandate, is expected to provide a clear action plan that will ensure that the transportation
May 10, 1990

links among Canada's regions are maintained and improved.
In making this announcement, the Prime Minister stressed the importance of taking into account the wide range of interests of Canadians and the respective roles of all levels of government and the private sector in the provision of inter-city services. He also emphasized the necessity to balance Canada's transportation needs with the government's policy of environmentally sustainable economic development.
The royal commission will examine Canada's unique social and democratic trends and look ahead to ways in which the transportation system must respond to meet the competing needs and demands of users, operators, employees and other interested parties. The commission is expected to provide Canadians with a blueprint for a comprehensive, co-ordinated passenger system to take us well into the 21st century.
All Canadians are aware that we must reduce the burden of the debt. Canadians have been asked to tighten their belts and VIA cannot be an exception.
This government has distinguished itself during the past four years through fiscal responsibility and judicious allocation of federal financial resources. When money is scarce, it has spent where it was most needed and most likely to produce results.
I invite members opposite and, indeed, all Canadians to look at the facts and to judge for themselves the validity of the fiscal realities under which we currently labour. If we have had to make difficult decisions, it is because in 1984 we inherited a legacy of debt, a legacy which I personally do not care to pass on to my children and to their children.
The difficult choices we have been forced to make have allowed us to reduce the growth of the deficit and bring the rate of inflation down to a more acceptable level. Responsible fiscal management combined with sound economic policies have paved the road to a rate of economic growth which rates among the highest in the industrialized world. As responsible Canadians we owe it to our children to leave them with every opportunity for development that we ourselves have enjoyed.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Fraser Valley East for letting me use his allotted time.
The goods and services tax will have a substantial, positive impact on all regions in this country, including the north, and more specifically, northern Ontario and northern Quebec.
The existing federal sales tax makes our products less competitive on foreign markets and favours imports over Canadian goods. This applies to northern Canada as well.
No fewer than 22,000 provisions and administrative arrangements have been required for a tax system that has only 75,000 taxpayers.
Furthermore, consumers have practically no way of knowing how much federal tax they pay when they purchase an item. Since the tax is applied at the manufacturing level, most Canadians don't even know they are paying the tax.
The federal sales tax is archaic and undermines the competitive potential of our economy. It must be replaced, and the federal government has made the requisite commitment.
The GST will differ from the existing federal sales tax in three respects.
First, the GST will apply to most goods and services, at a rate of 7 per cent. Because of its narrow base, the existing tax applies to only one-third of goods and services, at a rate that is normally 13.5 per cent.
Second, to collect the GST, only the value added to goods and services at each production and distribution stage will be taxed. Businesses will collect the tax on their sales to other businesses or to consumers, but they will obtain a full refund of the tax paid on their business purchases.
Third, the GST will be a visible tax. Its visibility consists basically in the fact that it will be applied at the retail level, to a very broad base and at a uniform rate.
That isn't true!

In this way, Canadians will know when they pay federal sales tax and at what rate.
Madam Speaker, the hon. member implies that the GST will increase the cost of goods, thus penalizing businesses located in the north, in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. In fact, northern businesses are now paying federal sales tax on a wide range of inputs, including fuel, vehicles, computers, office supplies, construction materials and communications. Even inputs that are exempt from the present tax contain tax components. Consequently, the existing federal sales tax adds substantially to business costs.

May 10, 1990

With the GST, businesses will be able to recover all federal tax paid on their inputs. All suppliers of goods and services who collect the GST on their sales will receive a credit for the tax paid on their inputs. The difference between the GST collected on their sales and the GST paid on their inputs will be paid to the federal government.
However, when the GST on purchases exceeds the GST on sales, the difference will be refunded to the business.
Merchants selling tax-free items such as basic groceries, prescription drugs, medical devices and goods and services for export will also be eligible for the input tax credit, even if they do not collect GST on their sales.
It is clear the GST will result in lower production costs, compared with the present system, and will improve productivity in all our regions, including the north.
It is often said that the positive economic impact of the GST will not be uniform across Canada, favouring Central Canada's manufacturing regions at the expense of other regions. In fact, the positive impact on the primary sector will be twice as substantial as on the manufacturing sector. We all know that the resource industry, including exports, is the mainstay of the economy of Canada's north, of northern Ontario and northern Quebec.
Long-term production gains for the primary sector as a result of sales tax reform will be 3.3 per cent, compared with 1.4 per cent for the manufacturing sector.
Furthermore, productivity in the transport and public services sector will increase 3.1 per cent, more than twice as much as the manufacturing sector.
The existing federal tax does not apply to manufacturers but to manufactured products. These are used everywhere in Canada, especially in those regions that are largely dependent on natural resources. In fact, the extraction and processing of raw materials involves to a considerable extent the use of equipment and construction materials. As I said earlier, Madam Speaker, these goods include substantial federal sales tax components, both directly and indirectly, thus increasing production costs and making companies less competitive.
Supply
The input tax credits will completely eliminate the federal sales tax on production and distribution. Buyers of equipment will see the cost of capital goods go down by about 4 per cent. This will result in increased production in northern areas, including northern Ontario, whose economy is heavily dependent on raw materials and exports.
The question of transportation costs has been raised many times. At present, the transport of goods is taxed indirectly since carriers pay tax on a large percentage of their inputs. These costs are reflected in the price of their services and ultimately in the retail prices charged to consumers. Under the GST, transport companies will claim the tax paid on their inputs and this will lower their operating costs.
Retailers and wholesalers will be better off because they in turn will benefit from the tax credit on inputs.
One of the most important features of the new tax is the GST credit, which is meant to protect Canadians on low and moderate incomes. Families whose annual income does not exceed $30,000 will pay less tax than they do now. Three quarters of families headed by a senior or a single parent will see their after-tax income increase once the GST is in place.
The GST credit is a simple and fair way to protect less fortunate Canadians. It helps those who need it most.
Madam Speaker, those who think the government is not committed to Northern communities are mistaken. The goods and services tax is fair and equitable because it will apply to all Canadians equally, taking account of their particular economic situation. This tax will bring the North considerable benefits, not only for businesses but also for individuals.

Mr. Speaker, this is National Forest Week. It is not too much to say that in Canada the forests are the environment. Of course, we all know that no subject is more important to the world today than the environment, and in Canada, no subject is more important to the environment than our forests.
If the concept of sustainable development is ever going to be applied successfully in Canada, it must begin with our forests. To put it simply, at least in my view, we must start the process of sustainable development by placing the forest map of Canada on the table with all of the players present, then we must decide in advance what we all want to accomplish. We must determine what our forests can produce and sustain over time and space, and we must reconcile ourselves to a consensus with society's interest in the balance. Only in that fashion will we be able to find a vision for Canada's forests which is both attainable and sustainable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, PRIDE is the acronym for Parents' Resources Institute for Drug Education. It was established in 1983 in Saskatoon as a response to the growing problem of illegal use of drugs in Canada.
It provides information, products and services for the fight against the inappropriate use of drugs. It is really a partnership among youth, their parents and teachers, as well as other professionals who have joined together to try to combat this growing menace.
It is supported by different organizations. For example, in my constituency, it is supported by school boards and schools. I note that the Norwood School Division, the St. Boniface School Division and the St. Vital School Division are supporters of PRIDE.
Right now between 1,500 and 2,500 young people and their supporters are in Winnipeg celebrating the sixth annual conference. This year's theme is "The 90s- Building a Drug-Free Canada".

Let us all work together for a healthy Canada by fighting drug addiction.

Mr. Speaker, while the Conservatives and Liberals continue to wage their turf war between the Commons and the Senate, tens of thousands of unemployed people continue to suffer the consequences.
Variable entrance legislation is necessary to balance the unemployment insurance coverage for those people who live in areas of high unemployment and to provide for them the benefits to which they are entitled.
Every day I get calls from people from all across Canada wanting to know why they are being penalized by these two parties when their families are without basic necessities because of this ping-pong game being played by the Parliament of Canada.

Cutting moneys to the New Horizons Program is not doing more for Canadian seniors. This government is not responding to the needs of our Canadian seniors. If anything, it is going behind their backs to cut the funding from such organizations as the New Horizons Program.

Mr. Speaker, since January, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his department have had a proposal from the inshore fishermen concerning the 1990 quota allocations in fishing areas 4X and 5, but they have taken no action on it. If the minister does not act within the next few days, he and his officials will have to accept responsibility for what happens.
These people are tired of being told that the stocks on Georges Bank must be protected when they see the Americans landing record catches on Georges, the offshore freezer factory ships within our waters and the foreigners overfishing.
I call on the minister to meet with the premier, who said yesterday to these people that he had to have a meeting with the minister as soon as possible to discuss this urgent crisis in the fishery. I call on the minister to meet with the premier before next week.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past months a number of strong public statements have called upon this government to demonstrate further prudence in its management and expenditures. Canadians recognize that we need greater symmetry between our fiscal policy and Canada's monetary policy. Both must be more supportive of the other.
It follows that further spending restraint can only be more supportive of the Bank of Canada's ongoing fight against inflation. These actions on the fiscal side, although often difficult, can only lead to much needed latitude for interest rates.
The task before us is to get on with it. The Auditor General and others have outlined opportunities for us to do so. I call upon all my colleagues to be more cognizant of the problems posed by government expenditures and to have an active interest or involvement in their reduction.
Our theme of the day should not be, "Crow must go", but rather, for the sake of our future economic growth, our theme should be, "Let's go with Crow".

Mr. Speaker, I rise to join my voice with that of a delegation from International Solidarity for Democracy in Guyana who are here today to call on our government to review its economic recovery program for Guyana. The disbursements of the program's funds have led to unrefuted charges of misappropriation, misspending and abuse by Guyanese government officials to secure their positions. Human rights abuses are legion.
An angry United States has threatened to withdraw its contributions to the economic program. It is time that Canada too made aid conditional upon the correction of these abuses.
The Guyanese president still refuses to provide audited accounts of how aid moneys will be spent. Resentment and frustration is widespread among the general public and economic disarray is evident everywhere. Emigration is escalating.
Effective economic recovery can only take place with a change in direction at the top. I urge this government to insist on free, fair, internationally monitored and supervised elections as a pre-condition for aid.

The federal transport minister's version of the American war on drugs is an unwarranted attack on the fundamental right to privacy of 250,000 Canadians who work in the transport industry.
In a media conference here yesterday, the Seafarer's International Union launched a public campaign to persuade the minister and his government to drop their mass urine testing strategy. Having sent empty vials to all government MPs, the SIU is now urging their members and Canadians everywhere to send urine sample bottles to the minister. Mr. Speaker, we are currently celebrating National Forest Week. The enormous contribution of pulp and paper, timber, wood panels and other wood products to our balance of trade is an impressive indication of the economic importance of Canadian forests. Mr. Speaker, this is National Nurses Week and, as in previous years, there will be an opportunity provided for members of Parliament to meet with members of the Canadian Nurses Association in the booth set up under the rotunda near the main entrance.
The more than 200,000 practising nurses in Canada are an integral part of the health care system and provide invaluable service in health care facilities, in the community and in the workplace. Their impressive contribution enhances the strength and effectiveness of our health care system.

To pay tribute to the nurses of Canada for their unique contribution to the health of Canadians, I ask my colleagues to join me in recognizing National Nurses Week.

Mr. Speaker, recently 30,000 copies of a brochure entitled Today It's Canadian Pork were published through Agriculture Canada. The purpose of the brochure was to advertise the Canadian pork industry throughout the United States.
At the last minute the brochure was scrapped and burned because of industry protests over the photographs which showed an inferior product, a product portrayed as unappealing, unappetizing and hardly conducive to selling pork.
The costly mistake, $30,000 of taxpayers' money, is just one example of profligate government waste. This mistake could have been easily avoided had Agriculture Canada consulted with the pork industry at all steps of creating the brochure.
How often do costly and careless mistakes like this occur and how many departments condone this kind of needless waste? Proper consultation between government and industry must be the rule, not the exception, where public money is being spent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and it concerns the contracting practices of the government.
Yesterday, in sworn testimony before the Disciplinary Committee of the Quebec Order of Engineers, former Conservative MP Michel Gravel said that he had personally given to a former cabinet minister, namely Roch LaSalle, thousands of dollars representing the proceeds of a party at which businessmen had contributed $5,000 each.
Has the minister looked into this matter? Has he satisfied himself that the highest conduct of behaviour was observed by the then cabinet minister and by the Department of Public Works in the awarding of its contracts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member would know, the RCMP is now aware, of course, of the allegations that were made yesterday. I am informed that the RCMP is looking into the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Deputy Prime Minister. Aside from the RCMP inquiry which, according to the Solicitor General, is about to begin I have the following question for the Deputy Prime Minister: Is he now prepared to ask for a royal commission of inquiry on contracts awarded by the Department of Public Works and the Department of Supply and Services between 1984 and 1989, as I have been asking in this House for the past four years? Yes or no? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure why the hon. member would want a royal commission of inquiry when the Solicitor General has indicated that the RCMP has taken cognizance of the allegations that have been made and they are investigating. What more does the hon. member want?

May 10, 1990
Oral Questions THE ENVIRONMENT

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of the Environment who is aware that global warming is probably the most serious threat we have ever faced. The minister knows that in Toronto in 1988, Canada, along with many other countries, adopted to reduce carbon dioxide emissions into the atmosphere by 20 per cent by 2005.
We know that the intergovernmental panel report will be out in August. We know that there is going to be a meeting in Geneva in November. What members of this Elouse and Canadians want to know in relation to the meeting that the minister is going to in Bergen is whether Canada will be moving on preliminary steps to stabilize the amount of carbon dioxide going into the atmosphere. The progressive countries, the countries that are alert to the nature of this threat, are seeking consensus and the United States is seeking to break that consensus.
Will Canada be on the right side of this issue or the wrong side?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will have the pleasure of being in Bergen in good company. As a matter of fact, it will be my pleasure to be there with two hon. members of the opposition and we are very happy to welcome them. I invited them with us because I felt this is a non-partisan issue and we should not repeat the kind of debate being discussed here in foreign countries. I trust that we have the full support of those colleagues.
This conference, I repeat, was never meant to announce specific commitments by any government on the CO2 reduction issue. It is a conference in view of the Brazil conference in the following the Brundtland commission report.
This government has made a commitment that in The Green Plan this fall there will be the announcement of targets and schedules to reduce CO2 emissions.
There are two reasons for doing this. The first is that all the countries in the world have said that they need to be provided with the IPCC report, in August, before making commitments. Second, we Canadians have engaged in a broad consultation process to learn what
Canadians think and expect in regard to CO2 reduction measures. We will respect the process. We believe that we must respect Canadian opinion, support and consultation on this. When we are ready, and we have announced that it will be in the fall, we will announce the commitment.
So we will not be there to create expectations. We will be in Bergen to support the countries, in view of the Brazil convention, and for the implementation of overall sustainable development measures.

Mr. Speaker, I think most members of this House are now aware that the implications of greenhouse warming mean that some entire nations on this earth could disappear beneath the surfaces of the oceans. That is a fact and it has been represented by many scientists in world fora.
My question to the minister is a very simple one and he does not need to beat around the bush. We have lost two years since Toronto. It is two more years until Brazil. During that four-year period we could have done a great deal to reduce particularly the amount of carbon dioxide emissions in the atmosphere.
Is the minister telling this House that while he is in Bergen on behalf of Canada he will support consensus for the reduction of carbon dioxide emissions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we will support the consensus to reduce CO2 emissions and we will support what was established as the process in Nordvik a few months ago, the necessity of making precise commitments after all the countries are provided with the IPCC report.
Let us remind people that this report will be the end result of a very important and intense effort to gain scientific knowledge and reach conclusions on the extent of the phenomenon of global warming.
I think before issuing such threats as the disappearance of countries under the sea, my colleague should wait until he has the report. We know that there is some measure of scientific uncertainty. We Canadians feel that, while we are uncertain, we must subscribe to an insurance policy and announce during the fall precise commitments in terms of reduction of CO2, and we will be doing just that. I can tell you that we will be one of the few countries in the world to do that.
May 10, 1990

My final supplementary question is for the same minister, Mr. Speaker. The minister has endorsed the Brundtland directive that full environmental assessments apply to both policy and projects in order to achieve sustainable development.
Can the minister assure this House that this will be fully honoured in the EARP legislation soon to be tabled in the House?

New measures are being drafted by the government and when they are ready, which will be very soon, certainly before the end of the session, we will announce what we have in mind and propose them to the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance.
In view of the fact that the Governor of the Bank of Canada has stated repeatedly that confidence in the Canadian dollar is one of the cornerstones of his monetary policy, and in view of the fact that representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and presidents of leading exporters in the pulp and paper industry and the mining industry are stating categorically that they need a reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar in order to survive, how can the Minister of Finance expect Canadians to be confident with the government's monetary policy when it is faced with such reservations by leading Canadian business leaders?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that these people are not saying anything other than what we are saying: the interest rates have to come down. Except, instead of believing in a rather magic or ill-defined solution as proposed by the opposition, we are using a monetary policy which is very clear, which is addressing the problem, and which will cause the pressures to come down in Canada. Then, with the inflationary pressures coming down, we will be able
Oral Questions
to lower the rate of interest and make sure that our economy continues to prosper.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the minister. Since the Governor of the Bank of Canada says he is not at all sure when the situation will be such that he will be able to lower interest rates, could the Minister of State (Finance) perhaps tell Canadians when the government is going to realize that its monetary policy is creating a disaster situation for Canadian exporters?

Mr. Speaker, I can inform the hon. member for Gloucester that inflation is the greatest threat to our exports, our economy and to progress in all our regions. He knows that perfectly well. We saw what happened under the Liberals, at the beginning of this decade, when we had interest rates in excess of 20 per cent and spiralling inflation. We don't want that to happen again. It is our policy, and we support the Governor of the Bank of Canada, whose policy is intended to take the steam out of an over heated economy that has been growing for six years and reduce the pressure, so that we can start a new period of growth in which our economy will make spectacular strides.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of State for Finance.
An information flyer is going out to every household in the country, at taxpayer's expense I might add. Its purpose, we are told, is to give some straightforward answers about GST.
The flyer states that Canadians pay $700 a year in hidden taxes. It neglects to say that Canadians will be paying $400 more a year in taxes after the GST is imposed and that this tax will probably be hidden in most cases. Does the minister realize that this pamphlet is misleading Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we would not print such a thing because it is not true. The tax reform we are introducing is excellent for

May 10, 1990
Oral Questions
the economy of Canada, particularly for the lower income family.
We have been receiving more than 250,000 calls-we simply believe our tax is getting to be more and more popular-asking us for information. We are providing it to Canadians, as the hon. member has indicated, but why should we go out of our way to tell things that are untrue? Families with incomes of below $30,000 will be better off after tax reform than they were before.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is right: the flyer does state that the GST credit protects modest income families, but studies by Global Economics have revealed that families with income under $30,000 a year will be worse off after the GST than they are now. Furthermore the tax credit is not fully indexed.

speechtext: Aha.

We are beginning to realize that our colleagues across the floor are beginning to believe us. They say that maybe they are telling the truth but it is not indexed. Maybe in a couple of years it will be different. They are beginning to see the light.
Another thing that they seem to forget is that the reform by the removal of a hidden negative tax for an exporting country like Canada will inject into the economy $9 billion of new activity. This is a very good thing for medium income families.

May 10, 1990

Why is the government going across the country to talk with Canadians on The Green Plan while, we learned in yesterday's leaked memo, it is making secret back room deals that are reducing Canada's commitment to the environment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:

In the last week we have conducted 30 information sessions during the consultation process. Just this week in Winnipeg we had more than 500 persons attending one of the information sessions. speechtext: The hon. member for Prince Albert- Churchill River.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. We see reports today that the minister and the Premier of Saskatchewan left their supper meeting yesterday with smiles on their faces. The farmers on the Prairies are not smiling because they are still caught in the phoney war between the federal and the provincial governments with respect to this long promised money.
The minister has argued that the provinces have to get involved to get more money to farmers. On the other hand, the farmers need that money now. Therefore, I ask the minister at what point he will end this game of arm-wrestling between the federal and provincial governments and get some money to the farmers, even if he
has to go it alone? When will they see some real money? When will there be some money in the hands of farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member, it was not a supper meeting, it was a meeting that took place yesterday afternoon.
We talked about the short term assistance package. We also talked at great length about the need for a long term stabilization and safety net. This is the subject of a committee which has brought down a number of recommendations for consideration by the ministers. We will consider that report at our meeting on May 18.
The Premier of Saskatchewan would like to see the short term assistance program phased into a longer term stabilization and/or safety net, which would provide the kind of confidence and security for the future.
I took the opportunity to indicate to him that the representations we received really reflect the multi-faceted nature of the problem. Most of the representations we receive in our office indicate that drought is the most serious problem.
There are other problems with respect to debt, the input costs. Low prices is one of considerations, but not the top consideration. I also took the occasion to stress to the premier the need for provincial government co-operation in terms of the design of the program, the delivery of the program and cost sharing. I think it was a very productive meeting.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture is aware that interest rate increases in the past two years alone have taken about $460 million out of the agricultural economy in western Canada.
Does the Minister of Agriculture not realize that this farm financial crisis is a result of reduced income and high debt, that he must release this $500 million that he has on the table immediately, if for no other reason than to make up for the losses suffered by the farm community caused by his government's high interest rate policy?

mean there could be $1 billion unleashed into the provincial economy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Forestry. Given the forestry minister's responsibility to protect the interests of the forest sector, and given the disastrous effects on that industry of the government's high dollar policy, what measures is the minister taking to help ensure that the high dollar will be lowered or, at the very least, what measures is he proposing to offset the harmful effects of this policy on the forest sector?

Mr. Speaker, as you know, the forest ministry has been equipped with a new forestry act, but it is not envisaged that this new act embrace the authority or jurisdiction over fiscal monetary matters.
I can tell the hon. member that we will continue to work closely in strategic partnerships with the provinces and the industry to make sure that through research, through the restoration and improvement of our timber stands, the industry can retain its health and dynamism.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
While the minister has admitted to us that he is unable to offer the forestry sector any relief for the high dollar value, could he at least tell us why the six Forest Resources Development Agreements have not yet been renegotiated? When will they be renegotiated? Why laugh at the industry and the provinces in such a way?

Mr. Speaker, some of the agreements have been negotiated and signed with the province of New Brunswick. The province of Nova Scotia has agreements. As to the other Atlantic provinces, some of the agreements are still in place.
Negotiations and discussions are continuing to get all the agreements throughout the country in place before they cause any disruption in the important task of
restoring and replenishing the areas of our forest land which has been overcut and not properly restocked.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance.
It concerns some straight-forward answers about the goods and services tax. I would like the minister to explain why the ad states that there is no impact on housing affordability when the government has already admitted that there will be an increase of $450 on a new home.
Other reliable organizations, particularly the Canadian Home Builders' Association, have documented that there will be an increase of at least $3,000.1 would like a straight-forward answer from the minister: Does he believe in truth in advertising?

Mr. Speaker, we say in this brochure what we have been saying from the start.
The impact of the GST on housing will not create an additional impediment to affordability, and this is the case. I could give the hon. member a lot of numbers. For example, the net effect on monthly mortgage payments on a typical house purchased in Halifax will $2 a month. The hon. member can tell me if this is really an impediment or incapacity to the affordability of houses.
In North Bay it will be $1 less, and in Regina it will be $4 more. This is the kind of impact we are talking about. The general impact will vary by about 1 per cent. This is not an impediment to the affordability of housing.

At least the government has been consistent.
Again today, the Canadian Home Builders' Association has asked the government to disclose the detailed calculations on the GST and the price of new homes. Again the government has refused.
Will the minister explain why the public should believe his figures when he consistently refuses public disclosure? What is he trying to hide?
May 10, 1990

It will vary from region to region, but on the whole these numbers are very precisely reported in the technical papers.
Certainly, it will not adversely affect the affordability of housing. That is nonsense.

legislation will be tabled before we break for the summer?
