speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the hon. member for Sudbury.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to address the motion of my party which states:
That this House condemn the government for its lack of commitment to northern Canada and for its failure to treat Northerners fairly and equitably-
I might add that with a motion such as this we could add all regions of the country that are not centrally located. Regions such as Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver seem to fare quite well.
May 10, 1990

We in northern Ontario suffer from a lack of proper transportation. VIA Rail services have been cut and we are all very much aware of that. This imposes great hardships on many communities in the north.
When the Conservatives came to power, they privatized Air Canada. As a result we now no longer have the benefits of Air Canada in any place in northern Ontario, except Thunder Bay. This means that we have lost some prestige. Some might say this took place because Air Canada was not making a profit in some areas. But I can tell you from my days on city and regional council in that area that we commissioned a study back in the early 1980s which proved to Air Canada that it did make a profit and it stayed on in the community.
With a lack of commitment to anything but privatization, Air Canada now feels that it does not have to worry about these markets. After all, we are captive market. We pay more and have less service, but there is very little we can do about it.
We have talked about the GST and the kinds of hardships that will be imposed on northern communities by it. Today, during Question Period, I spoke about a flyer and some straightforward answers about the goods and services lax. It mentions that in some instances consumers will have to bear the full brunt of the 7 per cent. It mentions dry-cleaning and movies, but the flyer neglects to mention that hydro and heating bills will bear the full brunt of the 7 per cent goods and services tax.
When one lives in a northern community, one's heating and lighting bills are high. The further north you go, the higher it is. There is no getting away from having to bear the full brunt of that goods and services tax. We have spoken with people from Ontario Hydro and the heating industries. There is very little manufacturers' sales tax buried in their rates now. There is no argument when these people say themselves that they are going to have to increase their fees because of the goods and services tax. They are sending out notices now stating that someone living in the north will have to pay far more because of this tax than someone living in the south.
Back in the fall, I asked a question of the Minister of Finance in which I explained that the goods and services tax will add a great burden on people in the northern and
Supply
more remote areas of the country because the cost of transportation will be taxed.
At that time, the minister was not completely aware of the effect of the cost of transportation on goods. He said that the merchants can claim a credit for the tax they pay on transportation. The fact of the matter is that the cost of transportation is included in the final price of the goods. The 7 per cent tax is added on to the final price of the goods. So, you do pay more if you live further away.
There is not only that, but your goods are less attractive. If you produce goods in the north, then you have to ship them. There is a higher transportation cost in the beginning to reach the larger markets. These people also have to bear the brunt of additional GST on a higher end result price. There is absolutely nothing in the GST that is of any use to people in Canada, especially not for people in northern Ontario and the more remote regions of the country.
There is no incentive for people to invest in some of the resource industries in the north. We have talked specifically about the cancellation of the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program. This was a form of subsidy for junior mining companies to go out and explore some of the sites in northern Ontario. The total amount of money now being spent on exploration has decreased, and decreased drastically. It will continue to decrease until only the large mining companies will be doing exploration. They will continue to do exploration. In 1987, we were benefiting from $1.2 billion in mining exploration. That figure will go down to about $400,000 by the year 1991.
We talk about retraining. We say people want to be retrained. Yes, they do want to be retrained, but they want to have a job to be retrained to. In a community such as Temagami there are the wood and mining industries. The wood industry is suffering greatly because of the 15 per cent surtax on softwood lumber. One of mining sites in Temagami was closed down just recently.
What do we say to the people of Temagami when we tell them we will retrain them? What are we going to retrain them to do if there are no jobs there? If we do not create incentives for people to create jobs in these areas, they are going to have to move. Do we tell a family: "Sell your house. Move to Toronto"? How can

May 10, 1990
Supply
they afford to buy a house or live in Toronto? These are very difficult choices that we must ask these people to make.
Furthermore, there are pressures in asking anyone to move to Toronto. There are pressures for social housing. It is not worth the incentive to move them to Toronto. It is far costlier to keep a person in Toronto than in an area where they have affordable housing.
The government has to change its mind-set. It has to decide that it has a commitment to northern Ontario, and to the regions of the country. It can do that, first, by enhancing diversification programs so that companies will be anxious to locate in these areas. Second, it can provide infrastructures such as transportation so that the goods that are produced in these areas can more readily reach the larger markets. That is absolutely essential. It is essential that all levels of government sit down together to map out some kind of plan. We cannot just say: "There is nothing we can do. Business will rule all." If business rules all, then there is no hope for anyone in this country. They will all move south.
I ask the government, please, to reconsider its stand. Any time there are any cut-backs in jobs at the federal level, offices in northern Ontario are closed. The Government says: "You can call Toronto or travel to Toronto, or you can travel to Ottawa". That is great if there are the facilities to travel and the money. But it does make the cost of doing business in northern Ontario much higher.
Just recently, Consumer and Corporate Affairs closed an office in Sudbury. All bankruptcies and trusteeships are now handled through a Toronto office and a Toronto number. This causes an additional aggravation which the people of northern Ontario do not deserve.
If there was any way possible to bring in some programs which would offer incentives for jobs to be created in northern Ontario, or in any of the other far-reaching regions of the country, then that would be the answer. Take the Atlantic provinces, for example, which are suffering. Thke some of the western provinces and their agriculture. There are problems there.
Perhaps the government will wake up and realize before it is too late that it has to consider seriously pushing Mr. John Crow into easing his high interest rate policy and letting the value of the Canadian dollar drop
somewhat to a more reasonable level. Then those exports which are vital to the northern communities would be allowed to trade at a reasonable profit and more jobs could be created.
I have to end my remarks now and say that, after this morning's meetings with Mr. Crow, I am not at all optimistic that Mr. Crow is going to consider reducing his pressure on high interest rates. I would think that Mr. Crow is watching the Toronto market and even the Toronto market is suffering because the manufacturers are shutting down in all these very important aspects of our economy.
I suggest that we condemn the government for its complete and total lack of action. It is not only a lack of action, but an action in reverse by cutting back programs to the regions. I ask that the government reconsider and give everyone a chance.

Madam Speaker, I wish to ask my colleague a question, after listening to her very enlightened remarks. She recognized the seriousness of the Conservative government's policies and the negative impact they have on the people living in the outlying regions of this country. These actions are really dividing us, not only rich and poor but also regionally. They are having a very negative effect on everyone.
When I travelled with the VIA Rail task force we were up in the Gaspe. I heard about the very serious problems that exist for the handicapped and for children in need of treatment who had to get to Montreal. I presume they would have to go to Toronto or other major centres if they come from other outlying districts. It is impossible to travel in comfort by bus, according to them, and I can understand that. Travel by car is often very difficult both in terms of the weather and in terms of the cost. Planes are very expensive, and I need not underscore that point.
What are people doing now that the services of VIA Rail have been cut? How are the needy, in terms of physical and mental health, seeking the kind of services that they require, let alone all the other aspects that you have looked at?

Madam Speaker, that is a very good question. I want to say to my hon. colleague that I have a nephew who is severely disabled. He was explaining to
May 10, 1990

me the difficulties he has in taking a bus. It is absolutely impossible for him to take a bus to travel to Ottawa or Toronto. For him to get on an airplane now is also very difficult because the Air Ontario planes are much smaller. There is very little room. They need a certain number of days for an advance booking. It is quite a procedure. It is a very demeaning procedure also, which I think is the most difficult thing of all for him.
There is no real way for him to travel except for his parents to transfer him to the car and drive him to wherever he has to go. The problem with this nephew of mine is that he is now in his thirties and his parents are now in their sixties. It is becoming much more difficult for them to do this for him.
Train travel was the answer for him. When there is a severe medical problem there are air ambulances and the like. That of course applies across the province of Ontario. It is a provincial initiative used only in extreme cases where a person's health is in danger. The Government of Ontario through medicare will help cover the costs of that. So in that sense he is protected.
It is the more mundane acts of ordinary living that are very difficult for these people. The lack of adequate transportation does not enhance the situation. It is a detriment to them becoming more mobile and more self-sufficient as they should be.
I thank the hon. member for that comment.

Madam Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak on this opposition motion.
When we talk about condemning the government for its lack of commitment to northern Canada and for its failure to treat northerners fairly and equitably, I want to stress that we are talking about all regions of northern Canada.
I want to start by telling Canadians about an experience that I had two weeks ago when I was in Graven-hurst, Ontario. I was speaking with people at Gravenhurst High School. We were talking about the environment. They were telling me that just three weeks prior to my visit the sewage treatment plant in the town of Gravenhurst, an antiquated plant about which they had been worried for many years because it was out of date and which, with the influx of population, was under
Supply
stress, broke down and spilled 100,000 gallons of raw sewage into Lake Muskoka.
There may be some who do not realize this but the Lake Muskoka region is one of the most precious assets of this country. At first blush many people would not realize how serious this was for the whole community. Here is a community that depends on the purity of the clean water for that region. If that tourism feature breaks down, then there is absolutely nothing left in the region.
What I am sensing is that there is a general lack of commitment to address northern concerns. It is almost as if we are paranoid about the deficit. We are cutting all the time and refusing to be creative, or we are being penny wise and pound foolish. I am not just talking about the national governments, all governments are responsible here. Had that sewage treatment plant been replaced two to five years ago this incident never would have happened.
There is a litany of examples like this across northern Canada where I think we are really being negligent. Yes, it is important to be careful of the deficit and debt of this country, but I also think we have to be creative. One of the great features of northern Canada is its value in terms of tourism. As you know, Madam Speaker, tourism is the biggest job creator in this country. If we fracture the stability of our tourism industry in this country, then we are in serious trouble. That is going to add an even further difficulty to the national debt.
Sometimes when I see some of the small cuts that the government is making in its programs, I get a sense that it is really not thinking long term. For example, in the area of tourism promotion, there have been massive cut-backs by this government. This is an area in which we should not be cutting back. We should be increasing the dollars that we put into the promotion of tourism in this country. With the GST coming we are going to need a lot more tourism advertising to lure people here because the GST is going to be a massive disincentive. That tourism factor touches every northern region of this country.
In other northern parts of Canada we have concerns about the environment at James Bay. We also have the concerns of the Cree to consider.

May 10, 1990
Supply
The James Bay project is the largest man-made project in the history of the world. We have to make sure that not only the rights of the aboriginals but also environmental concerns are fully addressed. We must put the government on notice that we are not just going to let some kind of a quick assessment of the environmental problems create a rush on the Cree causing them to lay back letting the decision of the provincial government and the national government be the rule of the day.
We have seen time and time again where these rights and the environment have really been compromised. Fortunately, right now we seem to have a government which seems to be getting a sense that the people of Canada are absolutely dedicated to making sure that our government and all people in public office are committed to the environment. I say that in light of this government's Speeches from the Throne and its recent green plan. This is another area where we must keep the government on its toes.
The same problem exists in Barriere Lake where we have had to press hard to make sure that the rights of the Algonquins are protected.
As we move across to western Canada, we see problems in Athabaska and the Great Slave Lake where there is great concern that the effluents from the pulp and paper mills will be flowing into the north as well, something which affects the fishery and the life of the aboriginal peoples there.
We have a real litany of concerns in northern Canada. We have a government that is not being as sensitive as it should be. These are precious assets for Canada, for all of us and for our children into the next 20 or 30 years.
If we lose our commitment to these areas, there will be billions of dollars we are going to have to-

Madam Speaker, as I was saying earlier, the government seems to be really missing the assets that we have in northern Canada. As I mentioned before we broke for Royal Assent, the greatest job creator in this country is tourism; our environment in the north, our water, our resources, our aboriginal peoples, Canada's first environmentalists are resources and assets that we cannot treat lightly. We cannot take them for granted.
This government always seems to be retreating from its responsibility, whether it is unemployment insurance, VIA Rail or selling off Crown corporations. One day the government states that they are being sold off because they are not making money. Then Canada Post makes money, but it is going to be sold off. There is a total lack of consistency in terms of its financial planning.
I am concerned that our north, right across Canada, is going to be put into jeopardy. We on this side of the House are concerned. As my hon. colleague from Thunder Bay said earlier, it should not be that just because a city in the north is having difficulty that we shut it down and move everybody to Toronto or to Montreal. That is not the spirit that built this country. We are here for equality of rights and we are here for disadvantaged regions in every part of Canada. We should not allow this government to enshrine its principle of treating this country like a business, where if something does not make economic sense today it is shut down and things are shuffled around like they are pawns on a corporate chess board. That is not the way to run a nation. It is certainly not the way to run the north.
We on this side of the House condemn the government for its treatment of northern Canada.

Madam Speaker, Earth Day was barely a week ago.

During the course of Earth Day, I had the occasion to meet a number of youth groups. I would say to my hon. colleague who comes from a large urban area like I do, you from Toronto and I from Montreal, that I was quite fascinated with these young people from an urban centre who were expressing serious concern. They wanted to
Supply
know: "Is it true, Mrs. Finestone, that the land mass that they are going to flood to meet Vermont, New Hampshire and New York's electricity needs is as big as France?" I said: "That is a very good question. I think so." They said: "But why are we doing that to our land? And is it true, Mrs. Finestone, that that is where the aboriginal peoples live? Did they not first come and settle this country? Are they not the first peoples of land? I understand that they have complained and they feel that their rights have been abridged."
The other part of the question, which they did not raise but on which I recall very heated arguments and exchanges in the House with the present Minister for International Trade, was with respect to water and the inclusion of water in the free trade agreement. We are all living with some concerns about the heat wave that is supposed to be coming, the desertification of our land, and the greenhouse effect. All these issues would indicate that we have to husband the waters of the north, take care in conservation and in planning and the directions we wish to go in terms of public policy.
I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood ran a very important seminar this summer which came out with some important decisions with respect to the environment. Did you address some of the questions that the young people asked me on Earth Day? Did you look at the implications of water in the free trade agreement?

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague from Mount Royal for the question.
The very first time I spoke in this House I mentioned that I was absolutely paranoid about the section relating to water in the free trade deal. The Government of Canada has stated that water is not part of the free trade deal. However, I have listened to some of the best lawyers in this country and they say the exact opposite. In fact Clayton Yeutter has said on many an occasion that the real jewel in the free trade deal is that they have access to Canada's water.
As I suggested almost a year and a few months ago, if the Prime Minister of Canada were so confident that water was not part of the deal, it would seem very simple to put all of us at ease. He has a very good relationship with the President of the United States. He could say: "The people of Canada are concerned about water in the free trade deal. Could I please have, Mr. President, a one-page special protocol letter, which you and I will both sign, saying that water is in fact not a part of this

deal?" I have yet to hear a response from the government.
The real sleeper in the free trade deal, the thing that we must all keep our heads up for, is the section related to water.
As for your first question that your students put about the environmental concerns and the rights of the Cree, we have been studying this problem for years and years. There are legal minds on both sides of the issue. The Prime Minister's former principal secretary is now lobbying on behalf of the party going against the Cree. When heavy-hitters such as that are brought in, there must be some legitimate concern.
It is incumbent on each and every one of us on this side of the House to make sure that not only environmental concerns but aboriginal rights and the rights of the Cree are protected. We should not only be catering to Hydro Quebec and the eastern United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this morning when I saw the Orders of the Day, I noticed that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River had put forward a motion. It almost reminded me of a shot gun type of approach into which he figured he would throw everything. However, Madam Speaker, he missed one thing. I thought for sure he would have condemned the government because we had a lot of snow in northern Ontario this year.
I have been here since 1982. I had the opportunity to sit in opposition between 1982 and 1984. If you are a Liberal, you never have to say you are sorry and you never have to say you are wrong.
When a motion such as this one is brought forward, it gives me a great opportunity to show the difference between 1982 and 1984, 1984 up to the present, and
exactly what changes have been made in northern Ontario.
Members of the House and those who are listening to this debate should go back a touch and focus on what has happened, because sometimes we forget.
Unemployment climbed from 358,000 in 1968 to
1,384,000	in 1984. That is before we were in power.
We have been hearing a lot about the bank rate in Canada in the last number of days and weeks. In 1981 it climbed to 21.24 per cent. The chartered bank prime was 22.75 per cent. A five-year mortgage was 21.75 per cent. If you are are a Liberal member, you do not have to say you are sorry. That is what happened up until 1984.
Let me review a couple of other fundamental issues just so we get this debate down to where it should be. Spending in the federal government climbed from $12.3 billion in 1968 to $109 billion in 1984. That is an average of 14.6 per cent. The deficit climbed from $400 million in 1968 to $38.3 billion in 1984. That is 96-fold increase. The debt of this nation climbed from $18.1 billion to $199.1 billion, an increase of 1,000 per cent.
You would almost think on September 5, the day after the 1984 election, just like a mushroom, all of a sudden it is the Tories who caused the deficit in this country, that there was never a deficit up until September 5, 1984. The truth hurts, but I think Canadians really have to understand why this government has had to make the changes it has.
We heard in the House today about unemployment. Let me review a few comparisons. In 1984 the annual unemployment rate in north eastern Ontario was 14.9 per cent. The annual unemployment rate in 1989 was 8.1 per cent. In northwestern Ontario it was 9.7 per cent in 1984 and 5.9 per cent in 1989. The unemployment rate in northern Ontario in 1984 was 13.6 per cent. That was after 15 solid years of great Liberal management. At the end of 1989, under a Conservative government-the bad boys, as they would like to convey to Canadians, and the people who do not know how to run the country-it was
7.5	per cent. I think those figure speak for themselves.
I would like to go through a couple of the areas that the member for Kenora-Rainy River wanted to talk about, for example, the lack of commitment to economic diversification in northern Ontario. Until 1984 if north-
May 10, 1990

ern Ontario wanted to deal with the federal government there was only one way to do it. We had to go to Toronto. Yes, we had a couple of offices in northern Ontario, but there was never a decision made in northern Ontario. The decisions were made either in Toronto or Ottawa, and they were usually too busy looking at booming parts of the country to worry about the concerns of dear old northern Ontario.
The Prime Minister, the minister for industry and trade at the time, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, and the cabinet decided that it was time that northern Ontario was recognized as an area of economic development with its own program. It is the first time that northern Ontario has been recognized. It was recognized with a program called FedNor. Offices were set up in Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, and Sudbury with boards made up of local individuals, people from northern Ontario communities who discuss and know what projects should go ahead.
Since 1984 this government has contributed over $19 million to the economy of northern Ontario. That is over 300 projects that ensure the opportunity for northern Ontario companies and communities to be able to have their own say and their own direction. That has never happened before.
We do not stop at that. We have never stopped. We are continuing to work along that line. I heard my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood talking about tourism. I recognize that tourism is very important to northern Ontario and this government recognized it.
On November 23 of last year the minister of tourism made an announcement of an $8 million contribution to FedNor to be specially earmarked for tourism. The maximum contribution allowed under the program is the lesser of $500,000 or 35 per cent of capital costs for theme parks, ski centres, tour boat operations. It is the lesser of $100,000 or 35 per cent of capital costs for accommodation and marina projects. This never happened before. This happened because local individuals on a board representing northern Ontario came to the government, talked to the minister and said: "We need
Supply
to have something that is going to help develop the infrastructure of tourism".
I would like to move on to another area we have talked about: the budget. The night of the budget it was put across northern Ontario by the opposition that FedNor was gone; the government had cut FedNor.
The government made one change in FedNor. That change is that projects over $100,000 will have an option which is plain and clear. It could be a loan repayable over five, ten or fifteen years on which no interest will be paid. If the board decides that that adjustment is not correct, it can be a straight grant. However, projects under $100,000 will continue to be seen as they were prior to the budget. We have increased FedNor by $14 million. Again I say to my colleagues who were crying wolf that they are wrong again. FedNor is strong. FedNor is there to support, and it will continue to support with extra dollars.
The part that is so troubling is that it is such a good program and that has been recognized. I wish the odd time my colleagues from the other side would take some time out and start to applaud it. The reason I say that is that I have a few figures here that I would like to place on the record.
Accepted FedNor assistance for electoral districts to April 12, 1990: For the riding of Algoma, 54 projects, $2,093,292 or 128 jobs created or maintained; the riding of Kenora-Rainy River, 36 projects, $1,386,660 or 148 jobs created or maintained; the riding of Nipissing, 20 projects, $3,855,994 or 425 jobs created or maintained.
FedNor has played an important part in bringing recognition to northern Ontario. The Marylin plumbing fixture plant will be built in North Bay, the first time a plant of this size has been located in northern Ontario. The efforts of the FedNor board and its employees enabled us to ensure that the infrastructure dollars were going to be there for that project.
I should mention that these are opposition ridings. They are not held by Tories. These are opposition ridings that this government believes in supporting. The Sudbury Nutrino Centre is a science centre, the only one in the world. This government has committed itself, from the Prime Minister with research and development, to the

May 10, 1990
Supply
minister responsible for FedNor, to the Minister of Science and Technology. We are committed to this project and to spending more than $30 million.
Two weeks ago in Thunder Bay we announced funding of $2 million to help get the Nordic International Games in Thunder Bay in 1995.
There are two other areas of FedNor I would like to take a moment to talk about. I have to watch how I say this, but we in northern Ontario have had a difficult time selling to the government, whether it is a stationery store, a furniture manufacturer, or a printing company. To be able to get on a list or to be able to get that opportunity at least to quote would be advantageous.
In 1986, under FedNor, we set up a procurement incentive program. An official based in Sault Ste. Marie works directly with the companies in northern Ontario to ensure they get the opportunity, are put on lists, and are informed of exactly who to call and how to fill out the quotation forms.
Furthermore, the Conservative government that members opposite would have people believe is so bad, will bring together on May 28, 29 and 30 here in Ottawa over 100 companies from across northern Ontario. They will be setting up displays, giving the opportunity for all departments to come and see what we have to offer in northern Ontario. That is a first. That, to me, indicates a real commitment to all the companies in northern Ontario.
There are areas in northeastern Ontario that are going through some difficult times. I can say that the town of Elliott Lake is having troubles. We are looking toward the advisory board and Pathfinders to ensure that everything can be done to help that community. My own riding of Timiskaming and communities within are certainly having difficult times.
Companies such as Dingwell's Machinery & Supply Company, which requires an investment of $430,000 will receive a FedNor contribution of $107,000 toward this sum. Company vice-president, Robert Bell, said:
FedNor was great to work with. They supported us throughout the
whole endeavour. They looked at it carefully to see if it was viable.
They looked for stability, and feasibility.
That is what economics is all about. That is what this program is all about. That is what northern Ontario is all about.
I would like to move on to one other area. It concerns the 15 per cent surtax on softwood lumber. There is no doubt that the lumber industry in northern Ontario is going through a difficult time. There are a number of reasons for that.
It cannot be blamed only on the 15 per cent surtax. If the hon. member over there would understand what the combination is and listen, I will tell him exactly what the reasons are. For instance, the logging and hauling costs combined account for 64 per cent of the over-all costs of operation. Poor timber quality results in higher cost factors. There are higher sawmill costs. There has been a 30 per cent decline in sales to eastern U.S. markets since 1986.
The province of Ontario, through the 15 per cent that they get back from the federal government, which is supposed to go back to the industry, received $30,551 million in 1987. In 1988 it was $21,358 million, and in 1989 it was $17,710 million. That totals almost $68 million.
That money should have been put back into the industry to help with modernization and silviculture and help them through the difficult times. Instead what did the province do with $68 million that belongs to the industry?
Madam Speaker, it is easy to talk but when you look at the facts, they are clear. To put the blame on the 15 per cent tax is not the answer. You must look at the combination of reasons why the industry is in trouble.
If my colleagues in Toronto at Queen's Park are listening, I hope they will lobby the Minister of Natural Resources to come to her senses and join in with the rest of the Canadian provinces and the forestry companies, to sit down and negotiate a way out of this. Of all the provinces, Ontario is the only hold-out before we can do anything to negotiate with the Americans. The province of Ontario is the hold-out, but I can see why. Who would want to get rid of a $68 million cash cow.
Anyway, I would like to move on to deal with a couple of areas.
We hear a lot about unemployment and the fact that the unemployment programs are not correct. We know that the other place is holding up Bill C-21, a bill that is so important for regions of this country. It is a bill that would give the opportunity for adjustments whether in mining, the sawmill and particle board industry, agriculture or the expenditure of $350 million a year for training for an additional 60,000 people who would like to be trained. Additional training is available for modern
May 10, 1990

technology, which is becoming more and more important to be competitive.
I should mention that this government, under the former minister from Kingston and the Islands, made the right decision in formulating Community Futures Program through which communities have the opportunity to ensure that the programs for worker adjustment are there.
I would like to take a moment to describe the employment, training and data programs that are ensured in ridings such as Timiskaming and Algoma in northern Ontario in order to show what this government is doing. In the year 1988-89, the riding of Algoma has received "$7,946,000".
Again, it indicates that this government is certainly recognizing that ridings such as these should be supported. Kenora-Rainy River received $7,645,584 for such programs as employment training, job development, job entry, Challenge 88, skills shortages, skills investment, Community Futures, Innovation.
Madam Speaker, if you listened earlier today, you would think there was not a thing that this government is doing in northern Ontario. We are doing everything we can, but this government was left with an anchor around the neck. There was mismanagement of the economy by a government that was in power for 15 years. It did not care about the future and whether there was a debt left for our children and grandchildren. Spend, spend, spend. Spending is popular because it gets one elected. Those days are over.
Canadians recognize that we have a problem and that we have to make adjustments, whether it is under the free trade agreement, on our tax reform or on the goods and services. This government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, is making the correct moves. We are making sure that we will be able to challenge Europe in 1992. Our country will be able to challenge anybody around the world with regard to manufacturing, ensuring that we have a strong structure in place for our children and grandchildren.
I say again that this government has done more to ensure the stability of northern Ontario and other

regions across this country in the last five years, and we will continue to do so over the next three years. I will say here right now that whether it is 1992 or 1993, Canadians are going to recognize what this government has done and that we have set the course for the next decade. They will be sure to elect this government one more time.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:

Madam Speaker, I also would like to pursue, with the member, the forestry agreement for British Columbia.

For the minister to-

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, prior to 1984, if someone in northern Ontario wanted to look into the expansion of a sawmill, an industrial welding shop, or a small business, their only opportunity would be to apply through Toronto. The applications went into a great big drum and, with any luck at all, at the end of the month, six weeks, or 12 weeks, they might have been recognized. In that period of time, there was so much red tape and so many hoops to go through that a year would be over.
May 10. 1990

One of our greatest concerns in 1984 was to ensure that we had a program in place so that individuals across northern Ontario, northwestern Ontario and northeastern Ontario, would have the opportunity to have counsellors who would move forward to ensure the programs were recognized and the applications received and reviewed by individuals in northern Ontario. This is what we tried to do.

Madam Speaker, on the point regarding red tape, I support the hon. member. I still think there is too much red tape, even though we have a place in the north. He did mention some interesting pluses which we recognize. The Sudbury Science Centre is one of them.
Some of these infrastructure commitments he made are interesting. A plant in North Bay produces toilets for houses and industry, but we are not building houses because the economy is not going forward and there is a whole spirit where the entire nation is lacking in confidence. This is where the member is missing the point we are trying to make.
The hon. member has an interesting list of statistics, but somehow they are not translating into moving the nation, turning on the nation, or getting the nation excited. He cannot use the argument that the government inherited a debt because, yes, we did have a debt but this government doubled it from 1984 to 1988 with one of the best economies we have had in years. The GNP went from about 450 to 620 in a four-year period. It was fantastic. That is when it should have been making some of its cuts.
When I was talking earlier about tourism, I was talking about marketing. We are going to have to stimulate and work twice as hard to get people to come to the north. The signal we are sending out regarding the problems we are having in terms of national unity and the GST is a bit of a nightmare for some American tourists.
For everybody.

We will have to do something totally different from what we have done in the past. This is what concerns the people and it is reflected in the fact that about 85 per cent of the people in the country at this moment lack confidence in the government. I dare say it could change and I am not being smug about that 85 per cent. It could bounce back a bit.

How does the hon. member respond to that feeling out there that shows a general lack of trust and confidence, in spite of all the statistics and contributions of the government, especially in the north? I will give the government credit also for other parts of northern Canada as well. I am more concerned about turning on the nation so that we can dream again and have feelings. Would he please address that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will make it quite short. The vast majority of the population in northern Ontario has a tendency to turn off when they feel that the comments being made are not really adjusted to what is happening.
I would like to make two small comments. With regard to the plumbing facility in North Bay, it is not only new houses that use new fixtures, it is an over-all market. The other part is that in that market-place we are also shipping into the United States. If this facility had not been built in North Bay, it would have been built in Illinois. It is an opportunity to export.
We also have a job to do in tourism. There are no two ways about it. We have a short season up there. If it is a good year, we might have eight weeks; if it is a a bad year, we are down to four weeks. So, we do have a job to do. Through different programs and opportunities, we have our tourist operators and associations going to the United States and southern Ontario with programs, starting off in mid-November through to the end of February. It is an effort that has to be made. Quite frankly, you cannot turn everything around at once. Through FedNor and other programs, we are doing everything possible and we will continue to do so.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today on the motion of the Liberal party. There are eight specific points mentioned in the motion, indicating the lack of commitment by the government to northern Canada and, from my perspective, northern Ontario, and the failure of the government to treat northerners fairly and equitably. It is demonstrated by the list which I think it is quite appropriate. But I do not think the list is all-encompassing. Very quickly, I jotted down at least two other areas in which the government's approach to

May 10, 1990
Supply
its policies has negatively impacted on life and the ability to survive in northern Ontario and northern Canada.
Let me start with one of my favourite topics, VIA Rail. That is a battle that northern Ontario residents fought as hard, if not harder, than other people across Canada. At 11.40 p.m. on January 15, we saw the last transcontinental train arrive and depart the Thunder Bay station. Well over 1,000 people who had attended a rally earlier that evening marched the half mile to the station to greet The Canadian.
Now, I should put into context that Thunder Bay is not a community that is known for visible protests. It is not the norm for its people to march on city hall in large numbers. We have a few committed individuals who, from time to time, are out there protesting certain actions by some level of government, but never in my lifetime have we seen over 1,000 people at 11.40 at night protesting a government policy.
It was important to them because it was not just a minor fine-tuning of the service. It was the out and out elimination of service. After that night, there were no more passenger trains rolling through Thunder Bay, Schrieber, Terrace Bay, Nipigon and Red Rock, Upsala, Ignace, Dryden, or through Kenora. We had lost 100 per cent of a service we had had for over 100 years.
Thirty thousand people got on and off in Thunder Bay with that service, but for the students at Lakehead University and Confederation College it was the only affordable method of travelling to and from our university and college community. People at the university and college have already noticed a decline in out-of-town student enrolment because of the cuts to VIA Rail.
It impacts on our seniors. Some chose not to drive or to fly to visit family and friends elsewhere in Canada, but others had no choice because of their physical make-up but to take the train. They no longer have that option. Residents of those communities in northwestern Ontario, who are confined to a wheelchair, no longer have an accessible means of transportation available to them, accessible in the sense that they can roll on and roll off by themselves. They did not have to have a stranger grappling with them to remove them from their chair to put them into a seat. They did not have to go through-let us face it-the insult of having to be carried onto a
plane or a highway bus. With trains, they did not have to go through that but now they do.
With the combination of the loss of VIA Rail, the deregulation of air, and the movement toward smaller and smaller commuter planes that are clearly not accessible for the handicapped, citizens in the smaller communities of northwestern Ontario have no choice but to relocate permanently to the Thunder Bays, the Winni-pegs, the Torontos and the Sault Ste. Maries, of this land.
The battle over VIA Rail was not just a romantic battle because we had had the train for so long. It was a key element in our ability to commute into and out of northwestern Ontario. The same applies to Atlantic Canada and northern parts of the prairies and British Columbia which were served by rail until this government decided that people were less important than the bottom line.
As you know, Madam Speaker, yesterday I was in the Federal Court of Appeal. We are waiting for a judgment on an action which I took along with Greenpeace Canada and my home community, the City of Thunder Bay. I mention that only to point out that decisions made here in Ottawa have far-reaching impacts on life-styles and on the environment. The government has argued in court not only that the Governor in Council or the cabinet is exempt from the environmental assessment review process, but so, too, is the Minister of Transport. If that is the case, what is left? Is the only person who has to adhere to an environmental assessment review process the typist in the steno-pool at Fisheries and Oceans? I hope not.
Just before I leave VIA to talk about some of the other items on the list of the motion, I want to read to you from a column that appeared in the weekend paper of the Times-News Chronicle-Journal of Thunder Bay. The writer is Gerry Poling, who is the regional editor for the paper and a life-long resident of northwestern Ontario and who has a really strong feeling about the north. He writes about his experiences post-VIA. He writes, and I quote:
In wiping out VIA Rail service to Thunder Bay, Transport Minister Benoit Bouchard, still left Canadians with a railway service across Canada, but via Armstrong. What he neglected to consider, however, is how one gets from Thunder Bay to Armstrong.
If you wanted to go to Vancouver by train, for example, you can buy a one way fare for $275 or, for seniors, $248. But then, to get to Armstrong, you have to take Grey Goose bus, which leaves Thunder Bay at 5:30 p.m. daily, and ride the 200-kilometre-long snakey, bumpy highway for 3 1/2 hours.
May 10, 1990

What he does not say is that that highway is the primary highway for hauling raw fibre from the bush. It is inundated with transport trucks, driving at very fast speeds, making a very unsafe situation for motorists and passengers in buses.
Just to continue, the cost for a one-way ticket is $24.20 or $38.70 for a round trip. Once you reach Armstrong you then have two hours and fifteen minutes to kill before train time, that is if the train is on time at 11.50 p.m.
He also points out that, by the way, the transcontinental train leaves Armstrong on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays only, so you must make sure you have the right day before you get on the bus.
The reality is that people are being forced to use alternate means of transport. More people are being put on the highways in northern Ontario, highways that have been killing people on a systematic basis for many years.
Highways don't kill people.

The hon. member chuckles but the carnage on those highways, because of conflicts between transports and private automobiles, is very serious. More than a dozen people a year, not just from northwestern Ontario but from across Canada, are killed in traffic accidents. The more people that are put on the highways, the more dangerous they become.
Let me leave VIA Rail and touch on some of the other aspects. With regard to unemployment insurance legislation, research that we have done shows that because of the changes to unemployment insurance-the reduction in the work weeks, the qualification period being longer, et cetera, upwards of $60 million a year is taken out of the northwestern Ontario economy. That economy is already struggling. We have communities like Atikokan, Ontario, in which one of every two people is out of work at some time each year and where there is a sustained unemployment level of 25 per cent.
Supply
The new UI act is not going to make it easier for them. Sure, they can get training, but for what? There are no jobs available. They have been through the training mill. They have had training for welders, log hauling, and for this, that and the other thing, but the jobs still are not there.
What northern Ontario and northern Canada needs is a more community-based form of economic development. We have to provide the tools at the local level to support the individual entrepreneur and to attract the investment group from outside. But beyond that, the north and, I would suggest, all regions in this country really need a better transportation policy.
I cannot put the onus on the federal government alone because transportation is controlled primarily by the two senior levels, provincial and federal, but the federal government does have a fairly major leadership role to play.
We hear these cries for Senate reform from western Canada and other parts of Canada based on the belief, and quite rightly so, that they have not been getting a fair shake. They see the jobs being created in the Golden Horseshoe and the greater Montreal area. Consequently, they see more government involvement visible in those areas. So they say to themselves that they need Senate reform so that they have some checks and balances and can get a fair deal, no matter what the stripe of the government in power, it will have to take notice of their needs.
There is a different way, and I think it is one that this House should explore from time to time to see how we can come up with a mechanism. It all stems around transportation.
One of the realities of the Golden Horseshoe is that because of the millions of people who live in that market it becomes cheaper to produce within that market the goods that that market consumes. The reason you cannot produce those goods in Thunder Bay, Atikokan, Calgary or Moose Jaw, is because of the high cost of moving those products from the manufacturer to the purchaser. That will always be a problem in Canada because of our geographic structure, that thin ribbon along the Ameri-

May 10, 1990
Supply
can border with a lot of drags south. We are seeing this now, not just because of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, but because of the natural forces of the economy between our two countries.
The solution is to find a way to neutralize the cost of transportation, to make it possible for the widget manufacturer who can sell 99 per cent of her product in Toronto, to also be able to make that product in Thunder Bay, Nipigon, or in Schreiber, and not find that it is impossible to compete with a Toronto-based producer because of the difference in the price of moving the finished product.
It may be a combination of the use of modes, a requirement that a good must travel by the cheapest mode, in other words, truck to rail to marine to final destination, so that you minimize the use of energy and maximize the saving to the producer.
The other way, which some companies already practice, is having a regional or national pricing policy. The best example in Ontario is beer. A box of beer costs the same on Yonge Street as it does in Kenora because the transportation component is rolled in as part of the wholesale price for the distribution. Therefore, everybody pays the same. Simpson Sears does it. Eaton's does it for a lot of their commodities on a regional basis. That allows them to market a fridge, stove, vacuum cleaner, or what have you at the same price in that regional market.
In effect, the purchaser in the Toronto area pays a couple of pennies more so that the purchaser in northwestern Ontario pays many dollars less. That is another method.
Another way would be to provide, through government intervention, some kind of tax credit system that would allow, again, for the neutralization of transportation costs. People may say that that is going to cause problems with those we compete with in the United States, offshore, and what have you, but as long as we are doing it for domestic purposes I cannot see any problem.
That is only a rough suggestion. I have not completely worked through the mechanics.
Would that not be a corporate tax rip-off?

No, it would not be a corporate tax rip-off because those who are being ripped off today would
finally get the benefits. It actually might help to lower the cost of housing throughout the province as well. The hon. minister might want to consider it from that point of view.
Let me deal with a couple of other areas because I realize that my time is almost up, but I would be more than happy to respond to members' questions about this concept I have put forward.
With regard to the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway, this government has recognized that the Western Grain Transportation Act, as adopted by the Liberal government before it, is having a negative impact on the port of Thunder Bay and other ports along the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway. This is another transportation policy which sought to equalize a particular mode of travel, in this case rail, in order to ensure an equal treatment in the movement of grain. The result has been a skewing of the system, a skewing of the marketplace, so that the west coast ports are favoured over Thunder Bay, Churchill and the Great Lakes system because the marine component is not included.
I realize that the Minister of Agriculture will be handing something down in June to deal with this, but it is a crucial matter to the port of Thunder Bay. We have gone from 1,700 or 1,800 grain handlers down to about 700. Men with 20 years of seniority did not get enough work last year to qualify for unemployment insurance under the old rules. So, Madam Speaker, work needs to be done in order to protect that component of the port of Thunder Bay, which allows it to be one of the few fully diversified communities in northern Canada.
On one final point, the member who spoke before me made reference to the contribution of the federal government to the World Nordic Games bid for the city of Thunder Bay. I was pleased that that happened. I supported the government and the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport all the way. I appreciate his help in securing that $2 million. I appreciate the help of some of his colleagues, particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister for Tourism and Small Businesses for their assistance in convincing Cabinet that it was important to assist Thunder Bay in its attempt to get the 1995 World Nordic Championships, which I know we will get in two
May 10, 1990

weeks, and Thunder Bay will once again be back on the map internationally.

speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know of the hon. member's interest in transportation because we have had many discussions on this in the past.
I know he would not want his comments to go by without also mentioning the fact that the government, realizing the need for a transportation policy in this country, especially on passenger transportation, has formed a royal commission on passenger transportation. I am sure that it will be looking to the needs for transportation for passengers in northern Ontario and northern Canada as much as it will in the Golden Horseshoe. In the Golden Horseshoe it is more a case of lack of capacity than a lack of ridership.
The member mentioned that people who are handicapped are not able to get access as easily now that the train has gone. I am sure that he will be glad to know that there has been a lot of investigation and, in fact, trial routes are now in place. Buses have been modified to give disabled people far more accessibility than the trains offered them in that they can be very conveniently lifted in their wheelchairs and put into place on the bus so that they never have to leave their chair.
I have spoken with disabled people who have tried this new system and they find it far superior to anything that they had before. It gives them far more ability to travel than they had in the past.
I know the member's concern about VIA Rail service in the north. I know how much effort he has put into it and I also know of his support for Thunder Bay and the port.
He raises a point about grain coming through Thunder Bay. I think he would also have to acknowledge the fact that part of the lack of grain travelling through Thunder Bay now is due to the fact that our markets for grain have changed. Much of our grain market now is in Asia and it is shorter to ship through the Pacific ports. That is one of the reasons why some of the grain is no longer going through the port of Thunder Bay.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. minister for her comments.
Supply
Let me start with the last one. The minister might be interested in knowing that grain from the prairies going through Vancouver is destined for Egypt and has to go through the Panama Canal.
The minister is correct that the markets have shifted. There is no question about that. There is also no question about the impact of the EEC getting its act together and becoming an exporter of grain. That has had an impact. What bothers me is that the Canadian Wheat Board is being more aggressive in seeking out markets in the Pacific Rim than it is, for example, in North Africa and the Soviet Union.
Admittedly, the mandate of the Wheat Board is to get the highest price for the lowest cost to the producer, and I have no objection to that. My party has long supported that concept. But that, in conjunction with the WGTA, has forced the Wheat Board to go that way. It has closed its office in Europe and opened a new one in the Pacific Rim. So I do not think it is fair to say that it is strictly market forces that have created that situation. There is also the drought. We have to admit that there just is not as much grain as we used to have. But the important point is that they are maximizing the west coast and using Thunder Bay for whatever is left over. Right now we are down to 30 per cent of the export trade, and we used to be at 60 per cent.
With regard to the bus modifications, yes, I am aware of those. I would have preferred that they had been in place across the system before there were any cuts to VTA Rail, because we have in fact disenfranchised a number of our citizens.
I found the minister's comments about southern Ontario interesting. I think she said their problem is lack of capacity, not lack of access. Perhaps another time she might like to explain why the Government of Canada, through its Order in Council, reduced the number of trains and the number of cars available in the southern Ontario component so that there is less capacity available. In the meantime it is going to sell off the rolling stock that VIA has declared surplus to its needs.
On a final comment, I will be appearing before the Royal Commission on Transportation to outline what direction I and my party feel Canada should be heading into the year 2000 and beyond.

May 10, 1990

Madam Speaker, I wonder what thoughts the member has with regard to the equalization of transportation costs. I think it is a great concept. Each province is taxing the diesel used by freight trains travelling across their province. This has been a tremendous deterrent for shipments, especially of coal from the western regions to the eastern regions. Has he any comments on that? That is beginning to be a very heavy burden on top of the other situations.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question.
Provincial tax on railroad fuel was one of the questions that came up time and again during the VIA Rail debate because VIA Rail is also charged that tax. It is interesting that that tax is really a road tax to assist in the maintenance and construction of roads within the provinces. The irony is that the one mode of travel that owns its own roadbed is being taxed on its energy consumption to help pay for the roadbed that everybody uses, not for free, but without paying the full cost.
With regard to the coal question. I know that my colleague, when he was here the first time, did a lot of work on the issue of coal from the Kootenays coming down through Thunder Bay, being processed there and going on to Ontario Hydro plants. I took up some of that work when I was elected in 1984, as I know did the hon. Deputy Prime Minister who heads a task force to examine coal.
Quite frankly, I am disappointed with the province of Ontario and my own provincial member, the Hon. Lyn McLeod, who is the Minister of Energy. The province decided not to purchase additional amounts of coal from western Canada, low sulphur coal I might add, a cleaner burning coal. It chose to continue to draw high sulphur coal from the United States to use in the Ontario Hydro generating stations. We will continue to push for that. Obviously, the elimination of the fuel tax on rail will be one of the ways in which we can help make western Canadian coal much more competitive with the American high sulphur coal.

speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to address the House today and to apprise it of this government's commitment, not only to the people of
the north but to economic development and diversification in northern Canada.
The current economic conditions in the north contrast sharply with those of the mid-1980s. In 1984, the economic indicators such as the GDP, value of production and employment still demonstrated the effects of an earlier economic recession. Today these indicators show signs of growth, due in large part to the joint federal-territorial economic development programs under the Economic Development Agreement.
We must, however, ensure that the improved situation today is sustained and that the current growth which has occurred, thanks in part to the policies and economic development programming that we have provided, continues.
In particular, this government recognizes that Yukon and the Northwest Territories must continue to strengthen their leading sectors and diversify into other sectors if they are to achieve greater stability in the future and provide northerners with an adequate number and variety of economic opportunities.
This government has undertaken a number of successful initiatives to help support economic development in the north and to provide a stable planning framework. From a policy perspective, it has provided greater certainty to northern developers by, first, reaching agreements in principle with northern native groups on outstanding land claims, by reaching agreements in principle with the territorial governments on a northern energy accord, and by introducing a northern mineral policy.
Through targeted economic development programming under the federal-territorial Economic Development Agreements, assistance has been provided to northern entrepreneurs and to organizations to investigate and pursue new employment and business opportunities. This programming has been successful because with minimal support the federal government is able to lever additional territorial government dollars along with project dollars.
It has also been successful because much of the Economic Development Agreement spending has been targeted at strategic priorities and projects that are now showing and will continue to yield definite long-term benefits. Importantly, infrastructure has been put in place in numerous communities under the auspices of
May 10, 1990

economic development planning subagreements. These subagreements have included renewable resources, mineral development, arts and craft development, small business development and tourist development.
Participation by native people and organizations as proponents of these EDA projects in the Northwest Territories has been significant. In the Yukon participation has been increasing but we know more can be achieved. The federal government has introduced the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, or CAEDS. This is to support native business and employment opportunities and to address economic development requirements of native people in general. With representatives from native organizations participating on the EDA committees, a greater understanding of the programming that is necessary has been gained with a resulting increase in usage.
The efforts under EDA to date have certainly made a positive contribution toward expanded, diversified and more stable territorial economies. However, to realize the full potential long-term benefits of the federal government's contribution to economic development, further government support and assistance is needed in the sectors that we have been encouraging.
Although the EDA with the Yukon expired last year, extensions have since been put in place. As well, the EDA with the Northwest Territories is scheduled to end this year. This government has, however, initiated preliminary discussions with both territorial governments with a view to developing new programming for a five-year period beginning in 1991.
The future challenge for the federal government in co-operation with northern governments is to continue the transformation of northern economies. This involves further diversification of the economic base with increased emphasis on sustainable economic development, structural changes to sectors, such as mining, to enhance the returns to the communities and to their residents, as well as linkages among the sectors.
Given the relative strength of the Canadian, Yukon and Northwest Territories economies and the possibilities arising from the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agree-
Supply
ment, it is easy to see that there are opportunities which can be pursued.
Under the subagreements of the EDAs, opportunities exist for the improvement and expansion of a number of essential areas, including the mining industry and the area of renewable resources, the tourism and business sectors, human resources development and skills acquisition, and ongoing economic planning by communities and governments.
The theme of diversification is not new. It has been a thrust of the federal and territorial economic programming in both territories over the last six years. We all recognize it as a solution to another challenge, which is to minimize the reliance upon a few sectors for revenue and employment.
Import substitution is a principal component of diversification, and the renewable resource sector is an excellent example of this type of development which will lead to stronger linkages between the wage economy and the traditional economies of the aboriginal people.
Technological innovation is another avenue for generating business opportunities, especially at a time when science and technology is a national and international growth area for future development.
Regardless of the approach taken to diversify the economy, long-term benefits can only accrue when economic growth has been balanced by the development and maintenance of a healthy resource base.
The key to this is the acquisition of requisite skills and training by our northerners participating in their expanding economy and the provision of an infrastructure achieved through community based planning which will encourage industry to locate and develop. This will be the key in the future.
I expect future federal economic development programming for Yukon and the Northwest Territories to recognize these many opportunities and to ensure that our efforts are directed to this accomplishment.
As well, this week the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development signed a roads program transfer agreement with the Government of the Northwest Territories. This transfer represents yet another step

May 10, 1990
Supply
made by this government in the development of responsible northern government.
With this transfer the territorial government will not only be directly responsible to its citizens for the existing roads system, but it will receive $10.5 million to do so. This is an increase from the original program budget of $9.4 million and effectively paves the way for increased access, development and exploration.
In addition to the further developments of the preceding sectors, there are other events which I foresee as having significance to the development in the north. These events include the North American air defence modernization project, the renewed interest in northern gas pipelines, and oil and gas projects in the Beaufort Sea. Opportunities for new or expanded businesses and employment will undoubtedly be generated by these endeavours.
These will be reflected in and complimented by the organization of the land use planning commissions and recently initialled final agreements to settle land claims for the Yukon Indians and the Dene-Metis as well as the agreement in principle for the land claim for the TFN.
The settlement of land claims will be of particular significance to each territorial economy. Obvious benefits will be derived from direct injection of funds into the economy as well as through any investments made by native development corporations. It also means that native people will have a substantial land base to manage and develop for their future. The future of the north will be one of co-operation in a common goal for growth and prosperity.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on this motion which I believe addresses a particularly important question, Canada's north.
The motion raises most of the critical issues that I believe need to be addressed. It speaks about economic diversification and the need for additional diversification. It points out that some of the transportation services have been reduced rather dramatically and it gives us the example of VIA Rail. It points out that some
of the transportation services have been dramatically reduced and it gives as one example VIA Rail. It also points to the regressive impact of the unemployment insurance legislation for high unemployment areas such as the north. Of course implied within that observation is that unemployment in the north is much greater than in a number of other areas in Canada. It talks about the planned cancellation of the northern residents' deduction. It identifies the imposition of the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber. It identifies the cancellation of the mining depletion allowance and flow-through share benefits for mining exploration and that the imposition of the goods and services tax will have a particularly negative impact on the north because of the higher costs involved. Of course 7 per cent is a great amount when we are dealing with costs that are higher than ordinary. Finally, it points out that there are no adequate adjustment programs for single industry towns.
How much do we really know about the north? I think this begs an even more fundamental or perhaps more basic question. How much we do really know about our country? How much do we really know about the province of Ontario if we have not lived there? How much do we really know about la province du Quebec, the Atlantic provinces, or the western provinces? How much do we really know about the north?
It has often been said that Canada is a country that does not know nearly as much about itself, its people, its regions, and its resources as it should. Therein lies a great problem.
I am particularly happy that this motion gives us an opportunity to talk about the north, one of the regions of Canada that is probably least understood.
When I think about the north right away I think about our two territories: Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I have been told that Yukon from a land mass perspective is roughly the size of Manitoba, which is approximately the size of France. In Yukon I am informed that there are approximately 25,000 people; in Manitoba, slightly more than one million; and in France, 55 million. I give these figures to show the dramatic differences that exist on this planet and in this country.
When we talk about the Northwest Territories, basically we talk about one-third of Canada's land mass. There
May 10, 1990

are just a few more than 50,000 people, people who identify with the Dene, Inuit and others; a mixed group to say the least.
When we talk about the north we must also include the northern part of many of our larger provinces, because they very much lie in the north. The north occupies much of Canada's land surface. It has much of Canada's mining, including gas and oil reserves. It has much of Canada's forests, water and soil. Without the north we would not only be a very small country; we would indeed be much poorer from a number of perspectives.
The north has a uniqueness, as I believe most areas and most peoples do, which is not very well understood. We often talk about small rather isolated areas, although that is not always the case. We often talk about small numbers of houses, residents, students, or whatever. However, there are extra costs that people do not understand as well as they should. Because of the large distances covered and because of the small numbers we do not get the economies of scale and indeed there are huge transportation costs. All people in the north want the essential services that are taken for granted in many of the larger of centres, such as a quality education system, quality health services, and social services which respond to the needs of the citizenry. That is fair. I think what this country needs to be all about is trying to make sure that those who do not have as much do have that which is necessary so that they can feel as if they are a full partner in this country we call Canada.
Recently I had an occasion to speak to some people in Inuvik, Iqaluit, Churchill and a number of other communities. I wanted to talk to them about the costs of bread, meat, fish, cheese, vegetables, fruit, paint, and fishing equipment. I took those at random because I wanted a sense of how much larger the costs were there than they are in Winnipeg, Toronto, Vancouver or Halifax. It was virtually impossible to draw any real mathematical relationship. Clearly it is much higher.
It was as much as four to twelve times higher depending upon the item and depending upon the locality. In conclusion, I was extremely surprised by that large gap, which I was told was mostly because of large transportation costs and because of the small numbers that are often purchased by the population that I have mentioned.
Supply
We need to address a basic fundamental question in the north, but it is essential to make a commitment to the provision of services equal to or equitable to those in other areas of Canada. I think whenever possible those services need to be on site or, whenever that is not possible, they need to be accessible. In other words they must be available. My first preference would be that essential services-health, education or any number of social services; I could go on-be there.
Like many other Canadians the people of the north want to feel part of this country. They want to feel that they are understood, that they are appreciated, and that what they have can make a difference to this nation. They believe they need the political power, not a disproportionate amount but sufficient that their regional development initiatives will be realized.
They want education that is comparable to other centres, school facilities, and teachers with training and experience who can do the kind of job and deliver the quality education so needed in today's society in order to be competitive and to contribute to one's community, one's province, one's territory and one's country.
They actually believe that there is no reason the quality of education should not be equal to those of other centres. As well, they are concerned about the post-secondary offerings, because clearly their numbers do not permit the construction of a college or a university in each centre, but they want access to that post-secondary education because they recognize how increasingly important it has become.
They realize that there are new technologies out there, new concepts such as distance, correspondence education which has been around for a while but which has been refined, campuses that can be set up, and people who can come in to assist in creating a more level kind of arena, a situation where they can get their fair share.
People in the north as I have defined it are aware of the special costs of transporting students to school, college or university; the special costs of books and equipment; and what have you. They are concerned about this matter. They want people in government who will appreciate that uniqueness and be ready to respond to it.

May 10, 1990
Supply
These people also believe as I do that there is a need for special opportunities to be provided so that they can be equal, equitable or competitive with others. There are a number of ways of doing so. Clearly it is not always to give the same; sometimes one needs to provide more in order to make sure that that is the situation.
