I appreciate your comments, Madam Speaker. I had understood that I had 20 minutes. So I have your permission to proceed, since I believe I have the support of my party. Thank you.

I was pointing out how important I felt it was that special opportunities were offered to those who life in the north. I was about to give an example of some programs in Manitoba, access programs which provided special opportunities to individuals who have now entered the medical profession, the law profession and other professions. This has provided role models for certain communities and groups that were particularly important. In other words, there is something that can be done. We have the proof that there is success in those kinds of programs.
As I pointed out initially, the motion addresses the whole issue of diversification. There have been attempts to be fair about the diversification of the north, but there needs to be greater opportunity and greater attempts undertaken in order to accomplish this very worth-while goal.
The economy of the north should be given an opportunity to diversify beyond natural resources and it can be done only if the basic infrastructure is in place. We need good roads, social services, and telecommunications
services. As one of my friends who wrote to me recently pointed out, not only do we need these good roads, social services and telecommunications facilities, "the north can be used as a base for high technology research into forestry, the environment and other areas."
I want to address the whole question of aboriginal self-government. It is time for us to make a full and total commitment to our aboriginal people so that they can become full partners in this country we call Canada. They need to have the political power in order to realize their goals, dreams and aspirations.
We have tried in a number of ways to help them, but that assistance has not been particularly successful if we look at where they are in terms of housing, education and a number of other factors. It is time that we took that step, that made the commitment, and that we explored openly and honestly the concept of self-government and greater autonomy for our native people.
I want to address the question of health care. It is easy to ignore that question in a sense by saying that these are small, isolated communities with few people, but it is not good enough. Clearly we cannot have a hospital in each centre. In fact it is impossible depending on the size of the centre to have medical professionals, but clearly we can have access to medical facilities available to people who live in our far outlying areas. It is absolutely essential to offer the kinds of medical services that we would find in other larger centres, as I pointed out either on site, if it is feasible, or accessible by air or any number of ways that may be adequate.
One of the questions that I think is important to raise is what does the north want? What would it like that it does not have today? I think the question is one that has been raised by most regions in Canada and by people in Canada generally. It is to be understood, to be appreciated, to have the political power and tools to realize its destiny and potential. It wants to be treated fairly and be able to participate fully in the planning of its future.

The Northern region is a misunderstood region that we do not know well at all as Canadians. It is rich, not only because of its people and its natural resources, but also because of its large potential that remains to be developed. It is somewhat fragile, from an environmental perspective. Caution must be used, otherwise long-lasting damage could be made. It is inhabited by people
May 10, 1990

who want to be given the opportunity to have their say in the decisions made which concern them in the Canadian governmental systems, whether territorial or provincial. They are people who have children, like you and I, and who want their children to have an education so that they can either go work elsewhere, if they wish to, or stay home and contribute to the development of their community.
I am referring not only to elementary school and high school, but also to post-secondary education. I understand, like many, that it is not always possible to have a community college or a university in a community, because of cost considerations for instance. Many other possibilities exist, however, through technology, through distance teaching and through allowing teachers from some colleges and universities to go and teach in small communities. It is also possible to invite students, as it has been done on several occasions, to come and study in colleges and universities in the south.
We nevertheless have a commitment to make. We must commit ourselves to providing them with education at home whenever it is feasible. These people want both an education system that will allow them to be competitive and other systems, such as health services, social services, etc. In general, I think that those people want to be understood, they want to be appreciated. They want Canadians to know that they exist, that they live in a part of the country that is extremely beautiful and extremely different from one side to the other. If you take, for example, the community of Lac la Martre and if you compare it to Iqaluit, Inuvik, Eskimo Point, Churchill or Dauphin, you will see enormous differences. But, nevertheless, there are great similarities. Those people want to participate fully in this country that we call Canada. The want to be partners who not only are appreciated, but who can contribute their talents, their energy and their resources.

Madam Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague on his excellent, well-prepared presentation. It seemed to me that there

is a long wish list for northern Canada and rightly so, because there is a definite problem there. I guess we can provide them with all the institutional requirements and schooling they need, but unless we give them a reason to remain where they are, we will see over the next 10 or 15 years a mass move from northern Canada to southern and western Canada and elsewhere.
One of the factors that will persuade the northerner to move is the GST. The goods and services tax is a reason for many northerners to think twice about remaining in the north.
In my view, we need to provide them with all the necessary services and institutions, especially educational, that they need. They should be provided with the required population in order to maintain and provide the taxation base they will need in the long run.
I would like the government to think about the immigrants who come to Canada using the business criteria for immigrating, somebody who applies with $150,000 or $200,000 and gets access to a visa to come to Canada. Perhaps the government might consider the creation of some sort of incentive to newly arrived business immigrants to locate in certain parts of northern or western Canada. This is one thing that can be done.
Also we have here in Canada many immigrants who come from eastern Europe, Asia, or Africa who are professionals, engineers or doctors for that matter. Those people are not allowed to practice in some provinces such as Ontario or Quebec or elsewhere. Maybe it is time for the government to make an assessment and look at the possibilities of encouraging those people to go to northern Canada and certain other parts of the country where they can practise.
There are many ways to skin the cat, Madam Speaker. I guess the most important element is that we have the will to encourage and help the people of northern Canada.
I would like once again to commend my colleague on his excellent presentation and I welcome his comments.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate some of the points raised with respect to responding to the north more sensitively perhaps than we have in the past and I would like to explore each of those.
I guess we have to start from a basic principle that I want to enunciate and repeat. That is, we need to make a full commitment to ensuring that people from the north have access to the same kinds of services that we have.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to address the House today on this opposition motion. I welcome the chance to clear up as well any misconceptions put forward by the claim that northern Canadians in any way receive less than fair and equitable treatment by the government.
In terms of Bill C-21, the new unemployment insurance regulations will, in fact, improve the effectiveness and the fairness of the current unemployment insurance program. It represents a natural evolution of a social program, an essential part of this country's compassionate ability to provide income security for those Canadians in all regions who are out of work and in need. It is part of our commitment to provide all Canadians, the north included, with the best training and adjustment programs possible.
We recognize the importance of the UI safety-net to many communities with seasonal industries, particularly in areas like the north and Atlantic Canada. Under Bill C-21, these areas will continue to benefit from the flexible entrance requirements tied to differences in unemployment levels.
I would imagine that the hon. member who spoke some time ago was referring to areas of high unemployment when he made his misguided statement about regressive UI legislation. It is wilful ignorance to suggest that plans to create a more active approach to unemployment and to build an efficient, competitive labour force would be carried out at the expense of Canadians with no prospects of finding a job. This simply is not the case.
Bill C-21 is explicitly designed to shield those people who live in regions of highest unemployment. This bill is designed to help, not hurt them.
Bill C-21, in conjunction with the new proposed boundaries for the country's economic regions, will make the unemployment insurance program more regionally sensitive. If anything, it will mean a more generous system for the north. The economic boundaries will better reflect the reality of today's regional work pat-
May 10, 1990

terns based upon previous unemployment figures, individual and family income levels, and regional industrial structures.
Yes, it may be true that claimants in northern Ontario will be affected by the bill. Some people will have to work more weeks to qualify for UI benefits, but to tag the legislation "regressive" does not do justice to the intelligence of the members of the House.
We were elected in 1984, and again in 1988, with a mandate that included controlling federal spending in order to maintain economic stability and continued growth, and to prepare Canadians for participation in the competitive global economy. Recent polls show that Canadians understand the government's efforts to make UI a more constructive, pro-active program.
Recent Decima polls and Environics studies show that about two-thirds of Canadians support the idea of using UI funds to train unemployed people so that they can find better, more stable jobs, and find them sooner.
It is foolhardy for anyone to suggest that Canadians do not want a more effective and efficient UI system. The Labour Force Development Strategy and Bill C-21 which flows from it is one means by which the government wants to use its resources better.
It must be kept in mind that the changes to Bill C-21 will free up significant resources and will result in reallocation of some $350 million to help claimants gain work experience and upgrade their academic qualifications while receiving benefits.
Eight hundred million dollars additionally a year will be made available for enhanced training and other re-employment measures which will enable more Canadians to find secure and lasting jobs. This is almost a 50 per cent increase in the $1.7 billion funding currently available. This is particularly beneficial to regions where the economy is more fragile and the need for skills and innovation is greater.
Two of the more successful government programs which offer important adjustment help to communities and businesses will also receive increased funding once Bill C-21 is proclaimed. The Industrial Adjustment Service, or IAS, effectively helps businesses and their staff work together on solutions to adjust problems. It plays a particularly important role in one-industry areas
Supply
that can be devastated by massive lay-offs or shutdowns.
At Dona Lake, Ontario, for instance, the IAS assisted the Windigo Tribal Council to ensure jobs for natives in construction site jobs. This agreement involved the provincial government as well.
In the Yukon at Elsa, a silver mine closed, throwing 200 employees out of work. Through an IAS agreement, social services support was provided, prospective employers were brought in for the purpose of recruitment, and resume preparation and job search activities took place.
Bill C-21 means that an additional $15 million will double the number of firms which receive help. That means 1,000 businesses instead of the current 500.
Another very important program is the highly successful Community Futures Program. It was designed to help small and rural communities which face chronic unemployment and economic decline. Towns like Hay River and Pine Point in the Northwest Territories, Sault Ste. Marie and Ear Falls in northern Ontario, and Fort McMurray in northern Alberta have all benefited from Community Futures.
The new UI bill will also add $50 million to this fund to help increase the number of communities which will benefit from the various options available. Some 200 additional rural and small town communities will be helped.
I would also like to mention briefly the maternity and parental benefits that will come into effect with the passage of Bill C-21. At present, maternity benefits are available for 15 weeks. This will be enhanced so that up to 30 weeks of benefits can be claimed. I know that many northerners are patiently waiting for these improvements to be put in place.
I can speak from personal experience with respect to phone calls that I have been receiving in my riding. I have received calls from Wanda, Belinda, Ken and Lori, Sharon, Greg, Shanna, Janis and Janet, just to name some of the people who have called me within the last couple of days. The question on their minds is: When oh when will this bill be passed? These are young parents expecting and anticipating to use one of the major benefits of this bill to provide for a basic opportunity to be good and proper parents to the new-born that they

are about to bring into this world. Having the 30 weeks, the double period of time available to them, means so much more to them.
Janet, the last woman whose name I mentioned, is of particular interest to me, not that one constituent should be any more important than another, but she is my daughter. She says: "Dad, when are you going to get that bill through?" I keep saying to her that we are doing all we can.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, a few words about the hon. member's magnificent speech, mainly about Bill C-21.
What is the connection between Bill C-21 and an opposition motion that says or appears to say that the Canadian government does nothing for northern regions? I think even Bill C-21 recognizes the fact that some regions should receive more than others.
Madam Speaker, as you know, Bill C-21 also provides for a new designation of economic regions. In Quebec, in more remote areas, this is extremely important, because often these communities are far removed from our urban centres and are more or less ignored. In the past, before Bill C-21, they were included with our large urban centres, and they were, in fact, terribly penalized because of the way the regional unemployment rate was
calculated. It was far more difficult for people to obtain unemployment insurance benefits or access to programs tailored to the needs of regions that are economically and socially disadvantaged.
Madam Speaker, unfortunately, Bill C-21, which was tabled in the House, is now being held up in the most partisan way by the Liberal Senate. This means we cannot implement measures that are adapted to today's needs, measures that will recognize the needs of isolated regions, of centres that need more government assistance than others. Unfortunately, because of the present delay caused, as I said earlier, by the Liberal Senate, all Canadians will have to pay the price.
And as far as the opposition motion is concerned, I read that the government is condemned for its lack of commitment to economic diversification.
Madam Speaker, when we look at what has been done in the way of job creation since 1984, and when we know that since 1984, 1.6 million jobs have been created in this country, 80 per cent of which are permanent jobs, I don't think this happened exclusively in our large urban centres.
When we look at the distribution of government funds among the provinces, it is clear that every part of the country has been affected.
When we look at what the government did in terms of decentralization- My colleague from northern Ontario was telling me that since FedNor was established, people in outlying areas can call on local officials and agencies without having to go to the large centres such as Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Victoria. Regional development is within their reach. And the government knew that, by creating agencies such as the Western Diversification Office, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and FedNor, implementing the Eastern Plan, signing the Canada-Quebec Agreement on Regional Development and providing funds for northern regions, it was decentralizing this money. It did it not to hinder but to promote the development of isolated areas because decentralization brings us closer to the problems. We are thus able to find solutions and make immediate decisions without having to go back through the system. I do not want to blame officials, far from it, but often when they get documents from a remote area, they are
May 10, 1990

not too sure where it is and what the problems are. Sometimes they say yes, sometimes they say no.
By decentralizing, the progressive conservative federal government has provided a great deal of services to the Canadian people.
The Opposition says that we did almost nothing for diversification. I want to remind them that since 1984, we have signed federal-provincial agreements with each and all of the ten Canadian provinces in most of the crucial economical sectors like agriculture, forestry, mining, transportation, all economical sectors that promote regional development, that result in the success or the failure of a region.
In Quebec, we do have some remote areas, although they may not be as far up north as some of those areas in other provinces. The federal government has been supporting Quebec's remote areas, especially its forest industry, with the Eastern Quebec Development Plan, put in place to assist what was considered a doomed region about twenty years ago, because of a perceived lack of economic activities and initiatives necessary for the survival of the communities. With Phase II of the Eastern Plan, the federal government injected close to $50 million to help entrepreneurs develop forestry resources which are vital and essential not only to the economy, but also to the environment. That gives you an example of what we have done.
As far as regional development is concerned, I mentioned earlier the Canada-Quebec Industrial Development Agreement that involved some outlying areas. Some funds have been frozen, if I may use that expression, to be used for those areas only. We have given them the opportunity to do more, to develop at their own pace, since sometimes remote areas cannot develop as fast as larger centres, not because of a lack of willingness of course, but often because of insufficient financial, human, and other resources. By implementing specific programs for those areas, the federal government has made a step in the right direction. But we still have a long way to go.
The government does not believe it solved all the problems of remote regions in Canada, nor does it intend to say it did. As we know, there are about 26 million of us in a huge country, we have to deal with long distances, a
Supply
small population and the whole economic question which, let it be said, is not always easy. Nevertheless, we signed agreements with the provinces, agreements which worked well, and this is new in Canada. Serious negotiations between the federal government and the provinces, strategies to share the more efficient spending of money between the provinces, the federal government, the institutions and the regions, are new indeed.
It wasn't easy, I admit, but the cooperation that had been lacking for several years was rediscovered at a negotiation table where there were frank exchanges of views and finally, we succeeded in many instances in doing more with less.
During those discussions, Madam Speaker, we came to recognize that there are some regions that need more intervention by the governments, where the amount of help cannot be arbitrary and has to exceed what was planned or what is considered to be the national average.
Madam Speaker, I am happy I was directly or indirectly part of the process by giving my support to my governe-ment these last few years.
The forestry agreement is extremely important. Some hon. members said a few minutes ago that the federal government did nothing concerning the 15 per cent surtax on softwood lumber exported to the U.S. but I can say, Madam Speaker, that the-
There were discussions with each of the Canadian provinces, the majority of which, 9 out of 10, including Quebec, of course, and British Columbia, the two biggest softwood producing provinces, accepted to negotiate, to cooperate in order to find a solution where as the money, instead of going to the American Treasury stayed in Canada where it could be used to develop the forest sector.
Thanks to that kind of joint action and discussions we were able to better help the forestry sector.
Madam Speaker, I was quite amazed this morning when the hon. member for Algoma, who is usually such a good critic in agricultural matters, said that the federal government had done next to nothing for agriculture. Let me remind him that we have increased spending in agriculture by close to 600 per 100 since 1984.

Let me remind him also that this government that introduced a long term dairy policy, a policy long awaited since the early 1980s, but which the Liberal government did not want to give to farmers.
Moreover, I would like to remind him that this governement has done enormously for our Western Canadian producers in terms of spending, in terms of money granted as drought relief.
Finally, in all the intiatives the government has undertaken in the last few years, whether in agriculture, forestry, mining, natural resources or natural resources systems, it has always been present and taken its responsibilities, sometimes alone, often in co-operation with the provinces. That, Madam Speaker, has produced interesting results that allow us to say remote areas are getting more, will be getting even more in the future and will be able to look after themselves and develop to the full extent of their potential and aspirations.

Madam Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague for his great speech, particularly for the clarifications he has given us.
I would however like him to explain what he meant exactly when he talked about two provinces signing or approving that agreement. Could he clarify that statement for us?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry.
Earlier in the debate there was some concern expressed about some of the forestry agreements and the manner in which they were being worked on, whether or not there were any increases at all in budgets since 1984, and whether or not silviculture and working closely with the industry has been part of forest management. With it being National Forest Week, could the parliamentary secretary take a moment to bring us up to date on exactly what the department is doing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
I suggest this is a most important issue, Madam Speaker. If we fully analyse the Department of Forestry, we discover that since 1984- as a matter of fact, in 1984, our Prime Minister had made a firm commitment to give back to forestry the status it deserved. How did we do it, Madam Speaker? By increasing by as much as 300 per cent the forestry budgets, and through Federal-Provincial agreements which resulted in over $1.1 billion investments in forestry. It is important for us, Madam Speaker. We went even further, because we are often blamed by the Opposition members who kept on asking the Hon. Member representing Northern Ontario what he had done under such and such agreement? I wish to remind them that from 1984 to 1988, or 1990, depending on their renewal date we signed the agreements.
We promised to do more and to renew these agreements. That is what we did with New Brunswick. That is what we did also with Nova Scotia. That is what we did finally with Newfoundland. That is what we did under the Eastern Quebec Plan. Madam Speaker, when the Minister of Forestry stood up in the House and promised to renew the agreements, to maintain the level of investments and to ensure the economic development of the forest industry, I think he clearly indicated his major interests and concerns as Minister of Forestry. By the way, Madam Speaker, it was our government which re-established forestry as a full department, no longer
May 10, 1990

dependent either on the Department of Environment or the Department of Agriculture or any other. It is a full fledged department which assumes its responsibilities and will continue to do so in the future.

Madam Speaker, I am happy that my collegue from Champlain (Mr. Champagne) mentioned that this government created of a distinct department of forestry. Up to now, its functions where shared by several departments. This new department made it possible to have a greater concentration, more precise budgets, as well as a more equitable distribution of moneys. My collegue mentioned the provincial distribution, the federal-provincial agreements reached since we took power, and, of course, those signed with the province of Quebec, which has made the most of the money and the agreements to have a thriving forest industry.
There is still much to do, of course. But it seems we have been on the right track for the last few years, and that the policy stated once again by the minister is an indication that our forests are in good hands.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):

Madam Speaker, unusual though this may sound in terms of forestry, I hail from a region half of which perhaps is covered by trees, and we are blessed with this exceptional Canadian industry which creates hundreds of thousands of jobs. I should point out that since 1984 our government has been very active in the forest sector, not only by establishing a full-fledged Department of Forestry but also by signing agreements which have enabled the regions to develop. Madam Speaker, one is always juggling a number of roles in this place, but I am pleased have made it on time to raise with the government on this adjournment debate the response that I received in April 1989 dealing with the question of the safety of airlines.
On that day I raised with the minister the fact that at the same time that the House of Commons was considering the bill to amend and actually create the National Transportation Agency, the National Transportation Act, which is the vehicle for deregulation of air, primarily, that the government had in its hands documentation from its own senior staff which suggested that the government was not prepared to handle the ramifications of deregulation. By that, the document meant that they knew they did not have the staff to deal with the increase in the number of carriers that was clearly going to happen because of the experience in the United States where there would be a mushrooming of the number of airlines servicing points in this country.
We have seen it in my home community of Thunder Bay where we have tripled or quadrupled the number of flights in and out of the Thunder Bay airport. We have become a hub. What this document showed was that the government was not prepared in terms of having the right number of inspectors in place in the right places, nor did it have the other components of the kind of protection system that all of us in this House and all of our constituents expect to be there. We want to know that every time we get on a plane that that plane is safe. At the same time that this House was considering the deregulation bill, this report warned that Transport Canada did not have the trained bodies available to them in order to handle this influx.

May 10, 1990
Adjournment Debate
We saw that in the United States there was an increase in the number of accidents. We have had an increase in incidents of problems with airline safety. We have had at least one carrier grounded because of its unsafe operation and its licence pulled by the Minister of Transport. We have seen questionable practices.
We have ongoing a major inquiry into the Dryden air crash. Some of the testimony before that inquiry has suggested that inspection was extremely lax. We have had other evidence in northwestern Ontario that a detected problem with an aircraft in terms of its welds was detected by an inspector in Winnipeg and recorded but never acted upon and ultimately that plane crashed because there was not the inspection procedure and follow-up that Canadians used to take for granted.
I was chastised by the minister at the time I raised the question for always connecting safety with deregulation. Ministers of Transport, right from the hon. member who is now the Deputy Prime Minister, through the minister of trade to the former Minister of Transport and even to the current one, kept saying that safety shall not be compromised. However, the reality is that there is cut-throat competition and the banker breathing down your neck, ensuring that you make those payments every Friday. If it comes down to making a choice between buying that replacement part that just is not worn out yet, but is close to the end of its life span, or making your payment to the bank, because you know if you do not make the payment to the bank they are going to pull the plug and put you into receivership, you take the chance. You say it is rated for 200 more hours and common sense tells me to replace it now, but I cannot afford common sense.
The government was warned of this, not just by my colleague, the member for Regina-Lumsden, who has recently celebrated more than 21 years on the transport committee of this House, but by their own bureaucrats that, at the very least, they did not have the capability of monitoring the changes that would occur in the aviation environment.
It goes beyond that. At the same time that the government was pushing deregulation, which I should
remind the House was started by the Liberal government before them, they were cutting back on air traffic controllers, placing in jeopardy the people who travel and who live in areas around Vancouver and Toronto.
Madam Speaker, I know that you know that I could go on for minutes if not hours on this important matter, but I recognize that my time has run out. I thank you for your patience and with interest I am awaiting the response of the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government has said many times and it will continue to say that safety is our number one priority. Perhaps the problem is that the hon. member opposite does not like to accept the enormous success that has been the reality of economic regulatory reform. The promise of the National Transportation Act in 1987 that less regulation will result in competitive market forces thereby ensuring adequate service levels and the establishment of equitable fares, appears to have unfolded as envisaged.
It is important to note that two large carrier families have emerged, both of which effectively link together the opportunity for national, regional and local airlines. As a result, Canada now, for the first time, has two fully-com-petitive coast-to-coast networks providing intensive competition on heavily-travelled intercity routes and in local service markets. Yet, notwithstanding the development of the large carrier families, the ranks of independent air carriers continue to grow.
As far as the recent failures of some charter operations, it is most misleading to blame deregulation for this. Economic regulatory reform created an atmosphere in which to compete. In a competitive world, there will necessarily be adjustments, and some growth and some failures.
Turning to the question of provision of resources, yes, Transport Canada as a whole has taken a cut in person years in some areas. This is nothing new. These goals were established in the 1985 budget with the government's commitment to reducing the size of the public service. These reductions are being accomplished in a number of ways, none of which will impact on the safety or the security of the travelling public.
May 10, 1990

These reductions to our human resources have been accomplished through a co-ordinated program recognizing and streamlining administrative functions, reduction of levels of management, consolidation of support services, increased contracting out and increased use of technology. It is important to emphasize that none of these will be affecting the department's ability to assure transportation safety and security.
In fact, the continued safety of the system is such an important issue that the former Minister of Transport established a task force in order to seek the expertise of the private sector, industry and government. The aim of the task force is to ensure that we have the right resources and that they are used in the right way in order to meet the challenging needs of the future.
The task force has been asked to look into the aviation traffic system and to provide the minister with recommendations on the approaches that will ensure safety standards are always maintained while improving the efficiency of the system to cope with the anticipated demands of the coming years and into the 21st century.
The member has forgotten about some of our recent initiatives, such as RRAP, CAEDS and MOS. I would like to say to him that we are very concerned and will continue to ensure safety and that the National Transportation Agency will undertake a complete review of the impact by 1992.

Madam Speaker, on April 9, I asked a question in the House about Lebanese refugees. I said to the minister that there were thousands of Lebanese here in Canada who had yet to obtain their refugee status and who were waiting for various committees to examine their files. I may point out, Madam Speaker, that the Lebanese are not the only ones, in fact there are a great number of people-I am particularly concerned about the Lebanese because I have had a lot of requests at my office and phone calls from Montreal. Many people from other countries come to Canada to live. Canada is a country of peace and opportunity, and it is perfectly normal that they should wish to live in this country.
Adjournment Debate
In the past, Canadians were always known for their generosity to immigrants. If I may look back, I would like to say something about the role played by immigrants in Quebec and how they were received, and in fact, I have first-hand experience. My father, who came from Lebanon in 1906 to settle in Canada and who went to Quebec was very well received. My mother, of French-Canadian and Irish ancestry, raised nine children. So we have a whole family, my father's relatives, his brothers who came over from Lebanon and were well received in Quebec-I think there are very few countries that can pride themselves, as Quebec does, on having welcomed immigrants with open arms. Look at the mosaic we have in Montreal! There we see that immigrants enjoyed the same benefits of prosperity as all other Canadians.
Today, there are refugees, like the Lebanese and Romanians I have met, and people from countries like Peru and Chile and Central America. They are all here in Canada, waiting for committees to decide whether they can stay.
I believe that perhaps one of the most important characteristics of a people is its generosity in receiving others who are seeking peace and trying to make a life for themselves, to have children and take advantage of opportunities they did not have in their own countries.
I would like to focus mainly on the Lebanese community, which is well represented in Montreal and elsewhere in Quebec and Canada. Since 1975, they have experienced a terrible war in their country. And I may add, Madam Speaker, that they were not fully responsible for that war. The Lebanese people themselves are not directly responsible for the civil war. They are involved of course, but look at the presence of foreigners, Israeli soldiers in Lebanon, Syrian soldiers in Lebanon, they have no business there. But as you know, it is not easy to expel them in this kind of conflict. And so there are thousands of Lebanese and especially children who have suffered the most and who are forced to live through these hostilities.
But some of them have been lucky, for it must be said that one has to be lucky to reach the island of Cyprus or flee elsewhere in the Middle East and eventually land on Canadian soil. I know that many of them did not come here through normal and legal channels. Some landed here with tourist visas and claimed refugee status. I can understand them. When you come from a war-torn country, it stands to reason that you would want to remain in Canada. Who would not? In committee I saw reports where these Lebanese people explained why

May 10, 1990
Adjournment Debate
they wanted to be given refugee status. Unfortunately they are told: Well, you have no sound motive to seek refugee status. Or else they are told: We do not believe your story. They are hardly in a position to know what really happened. When looking at a country destroyed by war, I would be inclined to believe that they are quite right to seek asylum in this land. That is why I made insistent representations by letter and by phone to the Minister's office to ask her not to return any Lebanese nationals to their countiy, at least for now. 1 say "their country" but it is shared by foreign armies. I am asking her not to deport any Lebanese citizens.
I would ask the same thing for victims of harassment, in Central America for instance. That is all. It is that simple, Madam Speaker. I am confident that the Canadian people will understand my request and I would ask those listening to my speech to send the Minister a letter saying: "Given the conditions in which these people live, especially the Lebanese but also Central Americans and others, those who are here should be given the chance to be heard. We should also find every reason to be as generous as possible and grant them refugee status so that they can live in peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the beginning of the civil war in the mid-1970s the Canadian government has with only brief interruption facilitated the immigration of Lebanese affected by the fighting who have close relatives in Canada.
The Lebanese special measures have allowed more than 17,000 assisted relative category immigrants to come to Canada under relaxed criteria. Many of those would not have qualified under normal circumstances or criteria. Together with those whose admission was authorized under normal immigration criteria, this constitutes a major contribution to the alleviation of the distress experienced by relatives of Canadian citizens and residents. The program is precisely designed to match Canadian efforts with the needs of those persons of
direct concern to Canada: those who are the relatives of our citizens and residents and those directly affected by the civil strife in Lebanon.
The hon. member knows that Canada withdrew its embassy from Beirut in 1985 because of the danger posed to Canada based staff. On April 27 1989 Canada opened a temporary immigration office in Nicosia, Cyprus in response to the influx of Lebanese to Cyprus. The office complement is now three Canadian visa officers, four Quebec immigration officers, and 22 locally engaged employees. Consequently, that office provides Lebanese applicants with a quality of service comparable or superior to any Canadian visa post abroad.
From the opening of the temporary office in Nicosia until April 5, 1990, that office issued more than 5,000 immigrant visas, 657 visitor visas, and 175 ministerial permits to Lebanese. To the end of March, our office in Damascus has in 1990 issued 1,668 immigrant visas and 227 visitor visas to Lebanese citizens.
Canada is the only countiy to have implemented such special measures and to have increased the levels of service in response to the flight of Lebanese nationals to Cyprus. Our response is both sympathetic and effective in considering the needs of individuals affected by the situation in Lebanon. We shall continue to assess the situation as additional issues emerge.
With respect to the immigration and refugee board, members of the board undergo extensive training to assist them in carrying out their responsibility of determining whether or not claimants are refugees as described by the 1951 United Nations Convention relating to the status of refugees. The acceptance rate for refugee claimants from Lebanon was 82 per cent in 1989.
